The last two conditions are usually plausible: they cite 10–20% capture in single-cell data. The first fails when stability, location, or sequence changes the chance that a molecule is seen; a bias that varies between samples makes the measurement negative binomial.

The three conditions are Box 1 of Sarkar and Stephens. The result is the law of rare events: many molecules, each captured independently with a small probability, give a binomial count close to a Poisson. A bias that is shared across samples can enter the Poisson model as a covariate; one that changes from sample to sample is extra noise. If a later protocol observes a larger share of the molecules, the measurement variance falls below the Poisson’s.

Going further. If sample \(i\) contains \(M_{i\ell}\) molecules of feature \(\ell\) and each is captured independently with probability \(p_i\), then \(Y_{i\ell} \mid M_{i\ell} \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(M_{i\ell}, p_i)\), and as \(p_i \to 0\) with \(M_{i\ell}p_i\) fixed this tends to \(\mathrm{Poisson}(M_{i\ell}p_i)\); writing \(M_{i\ell}p_i = s_i\lambda_{i\ell}\) separates the depth from the relative intensity. If the capture probability itself varies, \(p_i \sim\) Beta or \(\lambda\) varies between samples, integrating it out gives an overdispersed margin, the negative binomial for a gamma mixing law.

Negative binomial regression

Negative binomial · two parameters, one hierarchy

Keep the log link for the mean \(\mu\); add a dispersion \(\theta > 0\), the size in MASS::glm.nb. The count is a Poisson whose rate is itself a gamma draw.

Model

\[ \mathbb{E}(Y \mid x) = \mu, \qquad \mathrm{Var}(Y \mid x) = \mu + \frac{\mu^2}{\theta}. \]

Read the graph left to right: the mean comes from the linear predictor, the gamma draw lets each row have its own rate around that mean, and the Poisson is the counting. Large \(\theta\) means a gamma concentrated on \(\mu\), so the model returns to the Poisson. 📄 Townes reviews the count families in Review of probability distributions for modeling count data. Stress that \(\theta\) is not a second scientific effect to interpret.

Going further. With \(\lambda \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(\text{shape } \theta, \text{rate } \theta/\mu)\), integrating \(\lambda\) out of \(\mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda)\) gives \(\Pr(Y=y) = \frac{\Gamma(y+\theta)}{\Gamma(\theta)\,y!}\left(\frac{\theta}{\theta+\mu}\right)^{\theta}\left(\frac{\mu}{\theta+\mu}\right)^{y}\), Cameron and Trivedi’s NB2. NB1, \(\mathrm{Var}(Y) = (1+\delta)\mu\), has the quasi-Poisson’s shape and is a different model. Testing the Poisson against it puts \(1/\theta = 0\) on the boundary of the parameter space, so the likelihood-ratio statistic is a 50:50 mixture of \(\chi^2_0\) and \(\chi^2_1\) and the naive \(p\)-value should be halved (Self and Liang, 1987, Journal of the American Statistical Association).

Two sources of variance

\[ \mathrm{Var}(Y \mid x) = \underbrace{\mu}_{\text{technical: Poisson counting}} + \underbrace{\mu^2/\theta}_{\text{biological: } \lambda \text{ varies between units}} \]

Divided by \(\mu^2\), the squared coefficient of variation splits the same way:

\[ \mathrm{CV}^2 = \frac{1}{\mu} + \frac{1}{\theta}. \]

Deeper sampling raises \(\mu\) and shrinks the technical term. The biological floor \(1/\theta\) stays, however many reads you buy.

This is the reading that makes \(\theta\) useful. The Poisson part is the noise any counting process has; the quadratic part is the heterogeneity of the true rate between samples, enclosures, or cells. A Poisson dispersion statistic of 10.6 on CA-SYS says the second term dominates. In sequencing, \(\sqrt{1/\theta}\) is the biological coefficient of variation of edgeR (McCarthy, Chen and Smyth, Nucleic Acids Research, 2012).

Going further. The decomposition is the law of total variance of the next slide, read on the coefficient-of-variation scale: \(\mathrm{CV}^2(Y) = \mathbb{E}\{\mathrm{Var}(Y \mid \lambda)\}/\mu^2 + \mathrm{Var}(\lambda)/\mu^2\). A design consequence follows: once \(\mu \gg \theta\), more depth barely changes the precision, and more biological replicates are the only way to shrink the variance of a group mean.

The variance, by the tower rule

\(Y \mid \lambda \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda)\), with \(\mathbb{E}(\lambda) = \mu\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(\lambda) = \mu^2/\theta\) for the gamma.

\[ \mathbb{E}(Y) = \mathbb{E}\{\mathbb{E}(Y \mid \lambda)\} = \mathbb{E}(\lambda) = \mu \]

\[ \mathrm{Var}(Y) = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}\{\mathrm{Var}(Y \mid \lambda)\}}_{\mathbb{E}(\lambda) \,=\, \mu} + \underbrace{\mathrm{Var}\{\mathbb{E}(Y \mid \lambda)\}}_{\mathrm{Var}(\lambda) \,=\, \mu^2/\theta} \]

The law of total variance gives the negative-binomial variance without writing its probability function: a Poisson–gamma compound.

Two lines, both from conditioning on the latent rate. The Poisson contributes its mean as variance; the gamma contributes its own variance. McCullagh and Nelder write the extra term \(\mu^2/\alpha\); the alternative form \(\mu + \alpha\mu^2\) returns the Poisson as \(\alpha \to 0\).

Going further. The law of total variance, \(\mathrm{Var}(Y) = \mathbb{E}\{\mathrm{Var}(Y\mid\lambda)\} + \mathrm{Var}\{\mathbb{E}(Y\mid\lambda)\}\), holds for any latent \(\lambda\) with finite variance, so every Poisson mixture is overdispersed: \(\mathrm{Var}(Y) \geq \mathbb{E}(Y)\), with equality only when \(\lambda\) is constant. A log-normal \(\lambda\) with \(\log\lambda \sim \mathrm{Normal}(m, \sigma^2)\) gives \(\mathrm{Var}(\lambda) = \mu^2(e^{\sigma^2}-1)\), the same quadratic shape with heavier tails: the Poisson log-normal. Greenwood and Yule (1920, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society) introduced the gamma mixture for accident counts; Karlis and Xekalaki (2005, International Statistical Review) review mixed Poisson distributions.

Same mean, three values of \(\theta\)

The mean stays 8. Small \(\theta\) puts more mass in the tail, because \(\mathrm{Var}(Y) = \mu + \mu^2/\theta\). Large \(\theta\) collapses toward the Poisson. Illustrative, from scripts/generate-density-curves.R.

Cover the grey Poisson last. Ask which \(\theta\) matches a Pearson dispersion near 1. The answer is the large one. The CA-SYS \(\hat\theta\) of 29 is in that direction, not at 1.

One mean, two variance assumptions

Family Rate ratio 95% interval
Poisson 0.972 0.962 to 0.982
Negative binomial 0.971 0.941 to 1.002

This is the slide to slow down on. The point estimate barely moves, 0.972 against 0.971, because both models use the same mean equation. The interval is 3.1 times wider. Under the Poisson the contrast is “detected”; under the negative binomial it crosses one. Nothing about the biology changed between the two rows, only an assumption about the variance. Ask the room which interval they would put in a paper.

Going further. The near-identical point estimates are expected: when \(\log\mu\) is correctly specified, the Poisson score equations give a consistent \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\) whatever the true variance (Gourieroux, Monfort and Trognon, 1984), and the negative binomial only re-weights observations, by \(\mu_i/(1+\mu_i/\theta)\) instead of \(\mu_i\). The two fits therefore differ in efficiency and, mostly, in the covariance matrix. A third option keeps the Poisson estimate with a sandwich covariance, valid under any variance function but less stable in small samples (sandwich package). Ver Hoef and Boveng (2007, Ecology) compare quasi-Poisson and negative-binomial weighting and suggest plotting binned squared residuals against \(\hat\mu\) to choose between a linear and a quadratic variance.

Read the mean, then \(\theta\)

  • The rate ratio is a statement about \(\mu\), on the log link, per read
  • \(\theta\) is not a second effect; it describes leftover variation
  • With the wider interval, 1.00 is compatible with these data

A 2.9% lower rate under tillage would matter agronomically. These 595 samples cannot separate it from no difference.

The last line is the honest summary, and it is the pitfalls lesson applied to a real fit: the estimate is the result, and the interval says how much the data constrain it. Resist the temptation to call this a null finding. It is an imprecise estimate of a small contrast, which is a different sentence.

Same count, three implementations

  • Poisson
  • Negative binomial
  • \(\log(Y+1)\), then Gaussian

\[ \log \mu = \mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta} + \log(\text{library size}), \qquad \mathrm{Var}(Y \mid x) = \mu. \]

Tilled against no-till: rate ratio 0.972 (0.962 to 0.982). Pearson \(\chi^2/\mathrm{df} = 10.6\), so that interval is too narrow.

\[ \mathrm{Var}(Y \mid x) = \mu + \mu^2/\theta, \qquad \hat\theta = 29.3. \]

Same mean equation: rate ratio 0.971 (0.941 to 1.002). The interval is 3.1 times wider and crosses 1.

\[ \mathbb{E}\{\log(Y+1) \mid x\} = \mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}. \]

That coefficient is not a rate ratio for \(\mu\), and the library size no longer enters as an offset. The two means are not the same function of \(x\).

Arrow keys step the tabs. All three are fits to the CA-SYS reads, from generate-data-figures.R, using casys_teaching.csv.

Tab through Poisson, NB, \(\log(Y+1)\) Gaussian—arrow keys on slide. Rate ratio 0.972 vs 0.971, Pearson 10.6, \(\hat\theta=29.3\), log-plus-one loses offset interpretation. Script path generate-data-figures.R if asked.

The observation model is the margin

An expression model is a distribution \(g_\ell\) for the latent share \(\lambda_{i\ell}\). The observation model is the distribution of \(Y\) after \(\lambda\) has been integrated out.

A gamma \(g_\ell\) produces a negative-binomial margin. A point-gamma \(g_\ell\), a spike at zero plus a gamma, produces a zero-inflated negative-binomial margin. The Poisson recommendation is for the measurement layer. The margin is usually wider, because the latent share varies across samples.

\(g_\ell\) for latent \(\lambda\); integrate to margin of \(Y\). Gamma → NB margin; point-gamma → ZINB. Poisson recommendation is measurement layer; margin usually wider.

sctransform A · one negative binomial regression per gene

Each gene \(g\) gets an intercept and a dispersion; each cell \(c\) brings its depth \(n_c\), the total UMI count. 📄 Choudhary and Satija, Comparison and evaluation of statistical error models for scRNA-seq (2022), describe version 2.

Genes and cells are crossed, not nested: every gene is counted in every cell, so the two plates overlap on \(\mu_{gc}\) and \(Y_{gc}\). The model has no covariate of interest: it is a normalisation model, and the Pearson residuals it returns are the input of the downstream analysis. The next three slides are its three steps, on a simulated matrix of 1,500 genes and 800 cells, seed 20261005.

Going further. The original sctransform (Hafemeister and Satija, Genome Biology, 2019) fitted \(\ln\mu_{gc} = \beta_{g0} + \beta_{g1}\log_{10} n_c\) with both coefficients regularised across genes. Lause, Berens and Kobak (Genome Biology, 2021) showed that the per-gene slope estimates were unstable and that the analytic value is 1 on the natural-log scale: version 2 sets \(\beta_{g1} = \ln 10\) on \(\log_{10} n_c\), which is the offset \(\ln n_c\) on the slide, and keeps only the intercept and \(\theta_g\) per gene.

sctransform B · depth enters as an offset

The slope of \(\ln n_c\) is fixed at 1, so only \(\beta_{g0}\) is fitted. Doubling the depth doubles \(\mu_{gc}\); what remains is the rate per UMI, the same in a shallow and a deep cell.

Left: one abundant gene; its counts grow in proportion to the cell’s depth. Right: dividing by the fitted mean removes that trend. With the slope fixed, the maximum-likelihood intercept has a closed form, \(e^{\beta_{g0}} = \sum_c Y_{gc} / \sum_c n_c\), which is what the simulation uses. Illustrative, seed 20261005.

sctransform C · Pearson residuals stabilise the variance

\[ r_{gc} = \frac{Y_{gc} - \hat\mu_{gc}}{\sqrt{\hat\mu_{gc} + \hat\mu_{gc}^2/\hat\theta_g}} \]

Raw counts are heteroscedastic; after dividing by the negative-binomial standard deviation, every gene has a variance near 1.

Left: the variance of the counts grows faster than the mean, the quadratic term. Right: the same genes after dividing by the fitted standard deviation. Grey is what a Poisson model would give: abundant genes keep variances of 3 to 10, which then dominate a principal-component analysis. Residuals are clipped at \(\pm\sqrt{C}\), with \(C\) the number of cells, as in sctransform.

Going further. A Pearson residual has mean 0 and variance 1 under the fitted model; residual variance above 1 for a gene is then evidence of biological variation beyond the model, which is how sctransform selects variable genes. Version 2 also bounds the standard deviation from below, so a gene seen once or twice does not produce an enormous residual (Choudhary and Satija, 2022). Lause and colleagues (2021) show that with a shared \(\theta\) the residuals have a closed form and need no per-gene fit.

sctransform D · borrow \(\theta\) across genes

A rare gene has too few counts to estimate its own \(\theta_g\). The fit regresses the per-gene estimates on abundance with a loess curve and uses the curve instead. That is empirical Bayes: the prior is estimated from all the genes, then each gene borrows from it.

Version 2 leaves out genes with \(\sigma^2 \le \mu\) or \(\mu < 0.001\): they keep \(\theta = \infty\), a Poisson. Empirical Bayes in one sentence: estimate the distribution that the gene-level parameters come from using the data of all genes, then treat it as the prior for each one. Here the prior is a curve, and every gene is pulled all the way onto it. The intercept is regularised the same way in sctransform; abundance is the geometric mean, which is less sensitive to a few outlying cells. The simulation leaves 72 genes without evidence of overdispersion, seed 20261005.

Going further. In a full empirical-Bayes treatment each gene’s estimate would be shrunk towards the trend by a weight that depends on its own precision, as DESeq2 does for its dispersion on the log scale (Love, Huber and Anders, Genome Biology, 2014) and edgeR with its weighted likelihood. sctransform’s choice, replacing the estimate by the trend, is the limit of complete shrinkage; it is robust and fast, and it gives up any gene-specific dispersion that differs from genes of the same abundance. The trend is fitted on a subset of 2,000 genes sampled by abundance in the implementation.

Six count distributions, one map

Horizontal arrows integrate a continuous prior; vertical arrows condition on the total. Shaded nodes are the continuous members. Redrawn after 📄 Townes.

Read the top row first: Poisson to negative binomial by a gamma rate, the derivation of the tower slide. Then the left column: independent Poissons given their sum are a multinomial, which is what a sequencing library does by fixing the depth. The right column repeats the step with overdispersion, and needs a shared scale parameter. The bottom row is the compositional version of the top one.

Going further. If \(Y_\ell \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda_\ell)\) independently and \(m = \sum_\ell Y_\ell\), then \(\mathbf{Y} \mid m \sim \mathrm{Multinomial}(m, \boldsymbol\pi)\) with \(\pi_\ell = \lambda_\ell / \sum_k \lambda_k\), and the Poisson log-linear model with a sample intercept gives the same fitted proportions as the multinomial (Birch, 1963). Independent gammas with a common rate, divided by their sum, are Dirichlet; independent negative binomials with a shared scale, conditioned on their sum, are Dirichlet–multinomial. Shared shapes with different means do not stay in the family.

Compound, mixture, and the Tweedie line

  • \(\lambda\) fixed: \(\mathrm{Var}(\lambda) = 0\), and \(Y\) is Poisson.

  • \(\lambda\) continuous: a compound distribution. A gamma \(\lambda\) is the negative binomial. A normal draw for \(\log\lambda\) is the Poisson log-normal. Townes notes that this margin has a heavier tail than the negative binomial.

  • The latent discrete: a mixture. The zero-inflated model is the spike at a structural zero plus a count distribution.

Townes’s Poisson–Tweedie has \(\mathrm{Var}(Y) = \mu + \phi\mu^{p}\). The negative binomial is \(p = 2\). These margins generally have no closed likelihood.

Step three fragments: fixed \(\lambda\) Poisson; continuous \(\lambda\) compound (gamma NB, log-normal heavier tail); discrete latent mixture including ZIP. Tweedie \(\mathrm{Var}=\mu+\phi\mu^p\), \(p=2\) is NB; often no closed likelihood.

Independent counts, given their sum

Townes’s identity: independent Poisson counts, conditioned on their total, are one multinomial draw. If \(Y_\ell \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda_\ell)\) independently and \(M = \sum Y_\ell\), then

\[ \mathbf{Y} \mid M \sim \mathrm{Multinomial}\!\left(M,\; \pi_\ell = \lambda_\ell \big/ \textstyle\sum_k \lambda_k\right). \]

The same step with independent negative binomials that share a scale parameter returns a Dirichlet-multinomial. The shared scale is required. Negative binomials with a shared shape and different means do not, after conditioning, stay Dirichlet-multinomial.

A sequencing library is this conditioning. The Sarkar rate \(s_i\lambda_{i\ell}\) is the Poisson layer. Given the library size, the vector of features is multinomial. Modelling the counts as independent Poissons with an offset, or as one multinomial, are the two sides of that identity.

Poisson conditioned on \(M\) → multinomial with \(\pi_\ell=\lambda_\ell/\sum\lambda\). NB with shared scale → Dirichlet-multinomial; differing shapes break that. Library size conditioning is the sequencing identity.

Other count models

Poisson log-normal · a Gaussian latent on the log mean

Replace the gamma by a log-normal: \(\mathbf{Z}_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{m}_i, \boldsymbol\Sigma)\) and \(Y_{i\ell} \mid Z_{i\ell} \sim \mathrm{Poisson}\{\exp(o_{i\ell} + Z_{i\ell})\}\). The covariance \(\boldsymbol\Sigma\) carries the dependence between features. 📄 Chiquet, Mariadassou and Robin.

The figure’s \(\mu\) is the mean of the latent Gaussian; here it is \(\mathbf{m}_i = \mathbf{x}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol\Theta\), and \(\mu\) stays \(\mathbb{E}(Y \mid x)\). \(o_{i\ell}\) is the offset: twice the effort adds \(\log 2\). The likelihood has no closed form once \(\mathbf{Z}\) is integrated out; the paper fits it by a variational approximation, in the R package PLNmodels. The four corners of the figure constrain either \(\mathbf{m}\) (a known class, or a mixture) or \(\boldsymbol\Sigma\) (low rank, or a sparse precision).

Going further. Aitchison and Ho (1989, Biometrika) give the margins: \(\mathbb{E}(Y_{i\ell}) = \exp(o_{i\ell} + m_{i\ell} + \sigma_{\ell\ell}/2)\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(Y_{i\ell}) = \mathbb{E}(Y_{i\ell}) + \mathbb{E}(Y_{i\ell})^2(e^{\sigma_{\ell\ell}} - 1)\), the same quadratic shape as the negative binomial with a heavier tail. The covariance of two features has the sign of \(\sigma_{\ell\ell'}\), so unlike the multinomial the model allows positive correlation between counts.

A point mass of zeros is a mixture

A zero-inflated model is a different generative story. With probability \(\pi_0\) the observation is a structural zero. With probability \(1-\pi_0\) it is a draw from a count distribution \(f\). StatHarbor writes \(\pi_0\) as \(p\).

\[ \Pr(Y=0) = \pi_0 + (1-\pi_0)\,f(0), \qquad \Pr(Y=k>0) = (1-\pi_0)\,f(k). \]

A logit for \(\pi_0\) plus a log-linear Poisson is the zero-inflated Poisson. The negative binomial in \(f\) is the zero-inflated negative binomial. Neither is an exponential-family GLM.

StatHarbor compares a zero-inflated model with an ordinary Poisson by AIC, BIC, or a Vuong test, because those two models are not nested.

Going further. The zero-inflated Poisson is Lambert’s (1992, Technometrics); it is fitted by maximum likelihood, or by EM with the latent structural-zero indicator. Vuong’s test (1989, Econometrica) compares non-nested models through the mean and variance of the per-observation log-likelihood ratios. But the Poisson is the zero-inflated Poisson at \(\pi_0 = 0\), on the boundary, so the two are in fact nested there and the Vuong reference distribution does not hold; Wilson (2015, Economics Letters) documents this misuse. A boundary-corrected likelihood-ratio test, or a plot of predicted against observed zero frequencies, is the safer check. A hurdle model (Mullahy, 1986, Journal of Econometrics) tells the other story: every zero comes from one binary process and the positives from a zero-truncated count.

A zero is an observation

Sarkar and Stephens refuse the phrase “missing data” for a zero count. The picture: a minute with no cars at an intersection is a zero; an hour when the observer is away is a missing record. A sequencing zero is the first of those. Imputing only the zeros treats them as holes.

They also drop the word “dropout” for a supposed device that writes a zero whatever the true intensity. Spike-in controls, in the papers they cite, did not support a zero-inflated measurement model. A zero-inflated observation model can still be the right margin when the latent intensity itself has a point mass at zero.

Cars-at-intersection versus absent observer—sequencing zero is the first. No impute-only-zeros; spike-in evidence against dropout measurement model. ZI on latent intensity can still be right.

Four count models, three questions

Model Extra variance Structural zeros Exponential family
Poisson No No Yes
Negative binomial Yes No Only if the dispersion is fixed
Zero-inflated Poisson No Yes No
Zero-inflated negative binomial Yes Yes No

The practical line under the table: diagnose dispersion and extra zeros before you quote a rate ratio. An ill-matched family understates the uncertainty.

Table: extra variance, structural zeros, exponential family column. Practical line under table—diagnose before quoting a rate ratio. ZIP and ZINB are not GLMs in the strict sense.

Logistic regression

A binary response, on the logit

A binary response goes to a logistic regression. Here \(\mu = \pi = \Pr(Y = 1 \mid x)\). The logit is the link used here. The probit is the alternative they mention later, and it stays close to this curve.

\(\mu=\pi=\Pr(Y=1\mid x)\); logit link in the diagram. Probit mentioned as later alternative—stay on logit for odds-ratio reading.

Detection depends on how hard you looked

Methylobacter is a methane oxidiser, present in 35% of samples. The odds of detecting it multiply by 1.74 per standard deviation of log library size.

This is the logit on a real response, and the result is uncomfortable in a useful way: the strongest predictor of presence is not a treatment, it is sequencing effort. The tillage odds ratio from the same fit is 1.34, with an interval of 0.95 to 1.91, so it is not separable from no effect here. Any presence-absence analysis of sequencing data has to carry library size, exactly as the count model carries the offset.

What \(\beta_1\) does to a probability

\(\pi = \mathrm{logit}^{-1}(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x)\). A larger \(\beta_1\) makes the step steeper. \(\beta_0\) slides it. The curve stays inside \((0, 1)\). Illustrative, from scripts/generate-density-curves.R.

The steep curve is not a larger probability everywhere. It is a faster change. Ask where \(\pi\) is one half on the red curve.

Logit · only if \(Y\) is really binary

Detection of a taxon in a core is binary. A flux cut at an arbitrary threshold is the dichotomisation we have already rejected.

\[ \mu = \pi = \Pr(Y = 1 \mid x). \]

The mean of a 0/1 response is the probability.

\(\mu=\pi=\Pr(Y=1\mid x)\); flux dichotomisation rejected. Mean of 0/1 is probability—say it plainly before the simulated pH slide.

Logit · a simulated detection

\(x\) is centred pH, from \(-1.5\) to \(1.5\). \(Y\) is 1 if the taxon is detected.

\[ \mathrm{logit}(\pi) = \log \frac{\pi}{1-\pi} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x. \]

Fitted here: \(\hat\beta_0 = -0.32\), \(\hat\beta_1 = 1.44\).

At \(x = 0\), \(\hat\pi = \mathrm{logit}^{-1}(-0.32) \approx 0.42\).

Same seed, same script, still not a field dataset.

\(\hat\beta_0=-0.32\), \(\hat\beta_1=1.44\); at \(x=0\), \(\hat\pi\approx 0.42\). Centred pH \(-1.5\) to \(1.5\); same seed script, not field data.

Logit · the curve is the result

The band is for \(\pi\), not for a single core. A core is still 0 or 1.

logit-curve.R

fit_bin <- glm(y_bin ~ ph, family = binomial)
pi <- plogis(predict(fit_bin, type = "link"))

Two lines: fit on the logit scale, back-transform with plogis(). The saved figure is on the next slide.

Logit · the curve is the result

Stress that the band is for \(\pi\), not for a single 0/1 core. The code slide is excerpt only; the figure is the saved fit. Ask the room to say the estimand in words before they quote \(\exp(\beta_1)\). About one minute.

Logit · odds move by a factor, probabilities do not

A one-unit increase in centred pH multiplies the odds by

\[ \exp(\hat\beta_1) = 4.2 \]

Wald 95% interval: 2.4 to 7.4.

In this fit, \(\hat\pi\) goes from about 0.42 at \(x = 0\) to about 0.75 at \(x = 1\). That is a change of about 0.34 on the probability scale, not a 4.2-fold change in probability.

The interval is symmetric on the logit scale. It is not symmetric on the probability scale.

\(\exp(\hat\beta_1)=4.2\), Wald interval 2.4 to 7.4 on odds scale. \(\hat\pi\) about 0.42 to 0.75 is ~0.34 on probability scale—not a 4.2-fold change in \(\pi\). Interval symmetric on logit, not on \(\pi\).

The regression is for \(\pi\)

Olszewski places logistic regression in the generalised linear model: the target is a function of \(\mathbb{E}(Y \mid x)\). For a Bernoulli response that function is \(\mathrm{logit}(\pi)\), and \(\pi\) is the conditional mean. A classifier that thresholds \(\pi\) is one use of the fitted probability.

He dates the logit to Berkson, as an alternative to the probit, and the unified GLM to Nelder and Wedderburn (1972, their paper). In R the same statement is glm(y ~ x, family = binomial(link = "logit")).

Olszewski: logistic regression targets \(\mathrm{logit}(\pi)\); threshold classifier is one use. Berkson logit history and Nelder–Wedderburn GLM paper as on slide; R call family=binomial(link="logit").

A test of two proportions is this model

In the first of the two follow-ups, the Wald statistic for a difference of two proportions, with unpooled variances, matches the average marginal effect of a logistic regression with one binary predictor. The sampling scheme is two independent binomials, without a small-sample correction. He calls the algebra a conceptual bridge: the statistics match, and the note does not re-prove the asymptotic distribution.

The second note matches the pooled two-proportion \(z\), the statistic behind prop.test(), to the Rao score test of the same logistic model. Wald, score, and likelihood-ratio statistics agree asymptotically. The pooled statistic is the score test. Several grouping factors are an analysis of deviance for proportions, the GLM form of the deviance partition. A numeric covariate beside the group is the analysis-of-covariance analogue.

Part I: unpooled Wald matches logistic AME; part II: pooled prop.test matches Rao score. Several groups → deviance; numeric covariate → ANCOVA analogue links on slide.

Going further. For one parameter with log-likelihood \(\ell\), the Wald statistic uses the curvature at \(\hat\beta\), the score statistic the slope and curvature at the null value, and the likelihood-ratio statistic \(2\{\ell(\hat\beta)-\ell(\beta_0)\}\). Under the null all three are asymptotically \(\chi^2_1\), and they agree to first order under local alternatives; in finite samples they differ. The Wald version is the least invariant: it changes with the parameterisation, and for a logit it can lose power as \(|\hat\beta|\) grows (Hauck and Donner, 1977, Journal of the American Statistical Association). prop.test() applies Yates’s continuity correction by default; with correct = FALSE its \(X^2\) is the square of the pooled \(z\). Agresti sets out the three tests for GLMs (Agresti 2015).

One model, every test of proportions

A logistic regression, with its conditional, ordinal, and GEE friends, reproduces the classic tests of proportions and extends them with covariates. The worked list is the companion page.

Conclusion of the logistic block. Read the map clockwise from the blue box. What it replicates:

  • Wald’s \(z\) for two proportions with unpooled standard errors, via estimated marginal means on the probability scale, or the average marginal effect of the binary group indicator
  • Rao’s score \(z\) with pooled standard errors, which is prop.test(): anova(m, test = "Rao")
  • the \(\chi^2\) test for two or more proportions
  • an ANOVA-like joint test for several categorical predictors, and ANCOVA with numeric covariates
  • Cochran–Mantel–Haenszel for stratified or matched data, via conditional logistic regression
  • Breslow–Day for homogeneous odds ratios, via the Rao test of the interaction term
  • Cochran–Armitage for a trend in ordered proportions
  • McNemar and Cochran’s \(Q\) for paired proportions, and Friedman, via GEE with an exchangeable working correlation
  • Mann–Whitney–Wilcoxon and Kruskal–Wallis via ordinal logistic regression, and the paired Wilcoxon via GEE

The point is not to retire the named tests but to see them as special cases of one model, which can then take a covariate, a cluster, or an interaction.

Going further. The equivalences are exact for the score statistics and asymptotic for the Wald and likelihood-ratio versions: the Mantel–Haenszel statistic is the score test of the common log odds ratio in the conditional likelihood, and the Cochran–Armitage statistic is the score test of the linear term in a logistic model with scores for the ordered levels (Agresti, Categorical Data Analysis, chapters 3 and 6). The ordinal model’s link to Mann–Whitney is through the concordance probability: the proportional-odds coefficient for a binary group is a monotone function of \(P(Y_B > Y_A) + \tfrac12 P(Y_B = Y_A)\), close to \(\exp(\beta)^{0.66}/(1 + \exp(\beta)^{0.66})\) under that model (Harrell, Regression Modeling Strategies).

The fitting criterion is cross-entropy

Denis Burakov, in the chapter embedded below, starts from Fisher’s binomial likelihood and writes the average negative log-likelihood. For \(y_i \in \{0,1\}\) and fitted probabilities \(\hat\pi_i\),

\[ -\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[y_i\log\hat\pi_i + (1-y_i)\log(1-\hat\pi_i)\right]. \]

The factor \(1/n\) does not move the maximiser. This is the log loss, also called cross-entropy. In his table, \(y = 1\) and \(\hat\pi = 0.19\) costs \(-\log 0.19 = 1.66\); \(\hat\pi = 0.79\) costs \(0.23\). With an intercept in the model, the fitted probabilities add up to the number of observed events.

Burakov log loss: \(-\frac1n\sum[y\log\hat\pi+(1-y)\log(1-\hat\pi)]\). Table row \(\hat\pi=0.19\) costs 1.66 versus 0.79 costs 0.23. Intercept-only fitted probs sum to event count.

Going further. For 0/1 data the saturated log-likelihood is 0, so the binomial deviance is exactly \(2n\) times this average log loss: minimising cross-entropy and maximising the likelihood are the same fit. The log loss is a strictly proper scoring rule: its expectation under the true \(\pi\) is minimised only by reporting \(\hat\pi = \pi\) (Gneiting and Raftery, 2007, Journal of the American Statistical Association). The intercept property is one row of the canonical-link score equations \(\mathbf{X}^{\top}(\mathbf{y}-\hat{\boldsymbol\pi}) = \mathbf{0}\), so the fit is also calibrated in the mean within every level of a categorical covariate. The loss is unbounded as \(\hat\pi_i \to 0\) for an event, which is why one confident mistake can dominate the average.

The logit, rather than the probit

Burakov quotes Berkson’s reasons for the logistic curve over the probit: a closed-form derivative, fits that on Berkson’s data were as close as the probit or closer, and coefficients that exponentiate to odds ratios. A probit coefficient is a change in a standard normal deviate.

Angelino and Marcone add the complementary log-log link, \(\log\{-\log(1-\pi)\} = \mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}\), for a curve that is asymmetric about \(1/2\). They report that probit and complementary log-log fits are often close to the logit. The link on these slides stays the logit, so that \(\beta_1\) remains a change in log odds.

Berkson reasons on slide: derivative, fit quality, odds ratios. Complementary log-log for asymmetry at 1/2—probit and cloglog often close to logit. Deck stays logit for \(e^{\beta_1}\) reading.

Going further. All three links come from a latent continuous \(Y^* = \mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol\beta + \varepsilon\) with \(Y = 1\) when \(Y^* > 0\): a logistic \(\varepsilon\) gives the logit, a normal one the probit, an extreme-value one the complementary log-log. The standard logistic has standard deviation about 1.81, so logit coefficients are roughly 1.6 to 1.8 times probit ones (Amemiya, 1981, Journal of Economic Literature). The complementary log-log has a direct reading for detection: if the hidden count is Poisson with \(\log\mu = \mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol\beta\), then \(\Pr(Y > 0) = 1 - e^{-\mu}\) and \(\log\{-\log(1-\pi)\} = \log\mu\), so a library-size offset keeps its meaning and \(\exp(\beta_1)\) is a rate ratio. Near \(\pi = 1/2\) the links are close; they separate in the tails, where the data are usually thin.

One-hot coding is a contrast with a reference

Burakov’s worked table has 700 borrowers, 100 defaults. High delinquency: 80 defaults out of 180. Low delinquency: 20 out of 520. The model is \(\mathrm{logit}(\pi) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\), with \(x = 1\) for high delinquency.

The intercept \(\hat\beta_0 = -3.219\) is the log-odds in the reference group, a probability of \(0.0385\). The slope \(\hat\beta_1 = 2.996\) multiplies the odds by \(e^{2.996} = 20\). One category is absorbed into the intercept. The coefficient is the contrast with that category.

700 borrowers, 100 defaults; high delinquency \(\hat\beta_0=-3.219\) → \(p=0.0385\); \(\hat\beta_1=2.996\) → odds \(\times 20\). One category absorbed into intercept.

Softmax is the logit for \(K\) classes

For \(K\) mutually exclusive classes, \(\sum_k \pi_k = 1\), Burakov writes the softmax

\[ \Pr(Y = k \mid \mathbf{x}) = \frac{\exp(\mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}_k)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(\mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}_j)}. \]

Fixing \(\boldsymbol{\beta}_K = \mathbf{0}\) leaves \(K-1\) vectors. Estimating all \(K\) is the unconstrained softmax. The probabilities match. \(K = 2\) with a zero reference class is binary logistic regression.

Display softmax with \(\boldsymbol{\beta}_K=\mathbf{0}\) identification. \(K=2\) with zero reference recovers binary logit. Cross-entropy loss with 1-of-\(K\) indicators on slide.

Going further. The softmax probabilities do not change when the same vector is added to every \(\boldsymbol\beta_k\), so only \(K-1\) contrasts are identified; a reference class, or a penalty, resolves that. The fit is the multinomial logit, a GLM for a multinomial response (nnet::multinom in R). The odds between two classes, \(\pi_k/\pi_{k'} = \exp\{\mathbf{x}^{\top}(\boldsymbol\beta_k - \boldsymbol\beta_{k'})\}\), do not depend on the other classes: this independence of irrelevant alternatives is a strong assumption when two classes are near-substitutes (McFadden, 1974). For ordered categories, McCullagh’s cumulative-logit or proportional-odds model (1980, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B) uses \(K-1\) intercepts and one slope vector.

The chapter, on this slide

Denis Burakov, Logistic Regression: From Maximum Likelihood to Machine Learning, is the source of the loss, the weight-of-evidence arithmetic, and the softmax. The viewer scrolls the chapter.

Download PDF file.

Embedded PDF—students scroll Burakov for loss, WOE, softmax details. One sentence: this is reference material, not a live read-through. Keep timing short unless asked.

A Wald interval is a large-sample interval for \(\pi\)

Burakov builds the interval for a new covariate row \(\mathbf{x}_0\) on the logit, then inverts it. The covariance of \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\) is \((\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\), with \(w_i = \hat\pi_i(1-\hat\pi_i)\).

\[ \mathbf{x}_0^{\top}\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \pm 1.96\sqrt{\mathbf{x}_0^{\top}\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\,\mathbf{x}_0}. \]

The endpoints are symmetric on the logit. After the inverse logit they sit inside \((0,1)\) and they are not symmetric on the probability scale. The justification is the asymptotic normality of the maximum-likelihood estimator. A small sample, or the perfect separation on the checks figure, is outside that justification.

Build on logit with \((\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\); invert to \((0,1)\), asymmetric on \(\pi\). Separation and small \(n\) break asymptotics—link checks figure.

Going further. The interval is the delta method on the link scale, \(\mathrm{Var}(\mathbf{x}_0^{\top}\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}) = \mathbf{x}_0^{\top}\,\mathrm{Cov}(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})\,\mathbf{x}_0\); inverting the endpoints is exact because the inverse logit is monotone, which is why the band is built on the logit rather than on \(\pi\). A profile-likelihood interval, the set of values whose likelihood-ratio statistic stays below the \(\chi^2_1\) quantile, is invariant to reparameterisation and behaves better in small samples; confint() on a glm returns it in R (the method moved from MASS into stats in R 4.4.0). Under separation the profile is flat on one side and the interval is half-infinite, which is honest; the Wald interval is finite and wrong. Pawitan’s In All Likelihood develops the comparison.

Hold the other covariates still

With several covariates,

\[ g(\mu) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \cdots \]

\(\exp(\beta_1)\) is the multiplicative change in the mean, or in the odds, for a one-unit step in \(x_1\) with the other covariates held at the same values.

If \(x_2\) is a mediator or a collider, “held still” is a different estimand, not a more adjusted one.

\(\exp(\beta_1)\) with \(x_2,\ldots\) fixed at chosen values. Mediator or collider makes “held still” a different estimand—not “more adjusted is always better”.

Going further. The odds ratio is non-collapsible: adding a covariate \(x_2\) that predicts \(Y\) changes the coefficient of \(x_1\) even when \(x_2\) is independent of \(x_1\), and so is not a confounder, because averaging a logistic curve over \(x_2\) does not give a logistic curve with the same slope (Gail, Wieand and Piantadosi, 1984, Biometrika). The rate ratio under a log link and the risk difference under the identity are collapsible in that case. A conditional and a marginal odds ratio are both legitimate estimands, but they are different numbers, and comparing them across studies with different adjustment sets mixes the two. Greenland, Robins and Pearl (1999, Statistical Science) separate collapsibility from confounding; the mediator and collider cases are the causal-graph arguments of the Bayesian and causal section.

Two tiers of checks for a logit

🔗 The checks figure. A bent log-odds line, a variance-inflation factor above 5, separation, and fewer than ten events per variable are its warnings. Firth’s penalised likelihood is the remedy it names for separation. The next six slides take the checks one at a time.

The LinkedIn post is behind a login wall, so the thresholds are the figure’s own wording: VIF above 5 is a warning and above 10 a red flag; Cook’s distance above 1 is a cause for concern; ten events per variable is a rule of thumb the figure says some recent work relaxes. Angelino and Marcone’s Cook cut for a GLM is about \(4/n\), stated on the previous influence slide.

Going further. Albert and Anderson (1984, Biometrika) showed that the logistic maximum-likelihood estimate exists and is finite only when the two outcome classes overlap: under complete or quasi-complete separation some \(\hat\beta\) runs to \(\pm\infty\), and R reports fitted probabilities of 0 or 1 with huge standard errors. Firth (1993, Biometrika) penalises the log-likelihood by \(\tfrac12\log|\mathbf{I}(\boldsymbol\beta)|\), the Jeffreys prior, which removes the first-order bias and always gives finite estimates; Heinze and Schemper (2002, Statistics in Medicine) proposed it for separation, and logistf implements it with profile penalised-likelihood intervals. The ten-events-per-variable rule comes from simulation studies (Peduzzi and colleagues, 1996); van Smeden and colleagues (2016) argued that no single threshold guarantees good performance.

Logit check 1 · The log-odds are linear in each continuous \(x\)

The model assumes a straight line on the log-odds scale, not on the probability scale.

Fit a spline, splines::ns(x, 3), and compare it with the straight term. If the curve bends, keep the spline.

Card one of the figure. The check is about \(\eta\), not about \(\pi\): an S-shaped probability is exactly what a straight log-odds line gives.

Going further. The Box–Tidwell check adds \(x \log x\) and tests its coefficient; a natural spline with a likelihood-ratio test against the linear term is the more general version. Binned empirical logits, \(\log\{(y_k + 0.5)/(n_k - y_k + 0.5)\}\) against the bin mean of \(x\), give a quick picture. A missed bend biases the slope and also miscalibrates the predicted probabilities at the ends of the \(x\) range.

Logit check 2 · The covariates are not collinear

A variance inflation factor above 5 is a warning; above 10 the coefficients are unstable. car::vif(fit).

Collinearity inflates the standard errors of the coefficients. It does not spoil the predicted probabilities.

Card two. Students often drop a variable because its coefficient flipped sign; collinearity is the usual reason, and the fix depends on the question, not on the VIF alone.

Going further. \(\mathrm{VIF}_k = 1/(1 - R_k^2)\), where \(R_k^2\) comes from regressing \(x_k\) on the other covariates; in a GLM car::vif uses the weighted information matrix. For a factor with several columns the generalised VIF of Fox and Monette (1992, Journal of the American Statistical Association) is raised to the power \(1/(2\,\mathrm{df})\) to be comparable. Centring removes the collinearity between \(x\) and \(x^2\) or an interaction, but not between two distinct covariates.

Logit check 3 · The rows are independent

This is a design question, not a test. Repeated cores, plots, or dates need a random intercept, lme4::glmer(y ~ x + (1 | plot), family = binomial), or a cluster-robust standard error.

Card three. Point back to \(i\) inside \(j\): the number of independent units is the number of plots, not the number of rows.

Going further. A random intercept gives cluster-specific odds ratios; GEE (geepack::geeglm) gives population-averaged ones, which are smaller in absolute value by roughly \(1/\sqrt{1 + 0.346\,\sigma_u^2}\). On the latent scale the intraclass correlation of a logit model is \(\sigma_u^2/(\sigma_u^2 + \pi^2/3)\), because the standard logistic distribution has variance \(\pi^2/3\).

Logit check 4 · No single row drives the fit

Cook’s distance above 1 flags a row to inspect; \(4/n\) is a looser screen. cooks.distance(fit).

Refit without the row. If the conclusion moves, report both fits; do not delete the row silently.

Card four. The question is whether the conclusion depends on one plot, not whether the point looks odd.

Going further. Pregibon (1981, Annals of Statistics) gives one-step approximations to the change in \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\) and in the deviance when row \(i\) is deleted, built from the leverage of the weighted hat matrix at convergence and the Pearson residual. In logistic regression a high-leverage row is one with an extreme covariate value and a fitted probability not close to 0 or 1; rows with \(\hat\pi_i\) near 0 or 1 have small weight and therefore small leverage, even far out in \(x\).

Logit check 5 · There are enough events for the covariates

About ten events per variable is a rule of thumb, counted in the rarer outcome.

With fewer, simplify the model, or penalise it. Some recent work relaxes the rule; none removes the need to count.

Card five. Count the rarer of the two outcomes, not the number of rows, and count parameters, not variables: a five-level factor is four.

Going further. The rule comes from simulations by Peduzzi and colleagues (1996, Journal of Clinical Epidemiology); van Smeden and colleagues (2016, BMC Medical Research Methodology) showed that no single threshold controls bias. Riley and colleagues (2019–2020, BMJ and Statistics in Medicine) replaced it with sample-size calculations that target a small optimism in the fit and a precise intercept, implemented in the pmsampsize package. Penalised likelihood (Firth, ridge, lasso) reduces small-sample bias and overfitting but needs its own validation.

Logit check 6 · No separation, and no empty category

A zero cell, an odds ratio in the hundreds, and a huge standard error are the signs of separation.

Collapse a category that has no events, or use Firth’s penalised likelihood, logistf::logistf().

Cards six and seven of the figure: perfect separation, and the “one in the box” category with no events. Both are the same problem, one cell of the table is empty. R warns that fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred; do not ignore that warning.

Going further. Albert and Anderson (1984, Biometrika) showed that the maximum-likelihood estimate is finite only when the outcome classes overlap in covariate space. Firth (1993, Biometrika) penalises the log-likelihood by \(\tfrac12\log|\mathbf{I}(\boldsymbol\beta)|\), the Jeffreys prior, which always gives finite estimates; Heinze and Schemper (2002, Statistics in Medicine) proposed it for separation, with profile penalised-likelihood intervals. The detectseparation package checks for separation before the fit by linear programming.

What these three models do not cover

  • a zero-inflated count is the mixture already named, and it sits outside the exponential family
  • a composition is the conditioning on the library size; a log-ratio, after a deliberate treatment of the zeros, is a further model
  • a continuous flux: often a positive continuous distribution, or a Gaussian model on a scale you can defend
  • dependence in space or in time: the design block is next

Quasi-Poisson is a variance fix, not a full likelihood. Use it only if you can say what the interval means. 📄 A joint model for many species is the Poisson log-normal of Chiquet, Mariadassou, and Robin (the paper).

Bullet list: ZI mixture, composition conditioning, continuous flux, space-time design next. Quasi-Poisson variance fix only if you can interpret the interval—closing honesty slide.

Going further. Wedderburn (1974, Biometrika) showed that the estimating equations \(\sum_i (y_i-\mu_i)\,(\partial\mu_i/\partial\boldsymbol\beta)/V(\mu_i) = \mathbf{0}\) need only a mean and a variance function, not a distribution: this quasi-likelihood gives the Poisson estimates with \(\mathrm{Var}(Y) = \phi\mu\) and standard errors scaled by \(\sqrt{\hat\phi}\). With no likelihood there is no AIC; Burnham and Anderson’s QAIC divides the log-likelihood by \(\hat\phi\) as a workaround. The quasi-Poisson weights observations in proportion to \(\mu_i\), the negative binomial by \(\mu_i/(1+\mu_i/\theta)\), so on the same data they can give different estimates, not only different intervals (Ver Hoef and Boveng, 2007). For dependence in space or time, the generalised estimating equations of Liang and Zeger (1986, Biometrika) extend the same idea with a working correlation.

Two names, one role each

Angelino and Marcone (SIB, Lausanne, September 2026) use two roles. The response, also called the dependent variable, is what the model describes or predicts. That is \(Y\) on the notation slide.

The explanatory variable is also called an independent variable, a predictor, or a covariate. That is \(x\). The question picks it. The general line is \(Y = f(x) + \text{error}\). A function \(g(Y)\) on the left is a transformed response, which is the case the previous slides treat as a change of estimand.

Response \(Y\) versus explanatory \(x\); \(g(Y)\) on the left is the transformed-response case from earlier. Angelino and Marcone SIB attribution. Link notation slide if someone asks for \(\mathbf{x}\).

The link keeps \(\mu\) in range

\(\mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}\) can be any real number. The inverse link maps it into the support of \(\mu\).

  • \(\operatorname{logit}(\pi) = \mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}\) forces \(0 < \pi < 1\)
  • \(\log(\mu) = \mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}\) forces \(\mu > 0\)

A straight line on a transformed \(Y\) does not give the same guarantee on the mean of the original response. That is why the link stays on the mean, not on \(Y\).

Logit forces \(0<\pi<1\); log link forces \(\mu>0\). A line on \(\log Y\) does not guarantee a valid mean on the original scale—inverse link does on \(\mu\).

Going further. The fit is by iteratively reweighted least squares, which is Fisher scoring: regress the working response \(z_i = \eta_i + (Y_i - \mu_i)\, g'(\mu_i)\) on \(\mathbf{X}\) with weights \(w_i = 1/\{V(\mu_i)\, g'(\mu_i)^2\}\), and repeat until \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\) settles. With the canonical link (logit for binomial, log for Poisson, inverse for gamma), the observed and expected information coincide, so Fisher scoring equals Newton–Raphson and \(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{Y}\) is sufficient. The working response is a linearised \(g(Y)\), which is why the link never needs \(g(Y_i)\) to exist at \(Y_i = 0\). Asymptotically \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \approx \mathcal{N}\{\boldsymbol{\beta}, \phi(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\}\).

Equidispersion is one parameter doing two jobs

StatHarbor Analytics, Count Data Models: From Poisson to Zero-Inflated Models, starts from \(Y \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\mu)\) with \(\mathbb{E}(Y) = \mathrm{Var}(Y) = \mu\). One rate controls the centre and the spread. The log link makes a one-unit step in \(x_j\) multiply \(\mu\) by \(e^{\beta_j}\), a rate ratio.

The Poisson fit is the one they keep when the conditional mean is close to the conditional variance, the zeros are no more numerous than the Poisson predicts, and events are independent inside a fixed exposure. When \(\mathrm{Var}(Y) > \mathbb{E}(Y)\), the same fit understates the standard errors. They name unobserved heterogeneity, omitted covariates, and clustering as the usual sources.

Poisson: \(\mathbb{E}(Y)=\mathrm{Var}(Y)=\mu\); \(e^{\beta_j}\) is rate ratio on log link. StatHarbor list when Poisson is OK versus when SEs are too small. Heterogeneity, omitted covariates, clustering as sources on the slide.

Going further. Dean and Lawless (1989) derived the score test of \(\mathrm{Var}(Y)=\mu\) against \(\mathrm{Var}(Y)=\mu+\alpha\mu^2\); it needs only the Poisson fit, and its statistic is \(\sum_i\{(y_i-\hat\mu_i)^2 - y_i\}/\sqrt{2\sum_i\hat\mu_i^2}\), approximately standard normal under the Poisson. Cameron and Trivedi (1990, Journal of Econometrics) recast it as an auxiliary regression of \(\{(y_i-\hat\mu_i)^2-y_i\}/\hat\mu_i\) on \(\hat\mu_i\), without intercept, and test the slope. Overdispersion is not always heterogeneity: a missing offset, clustering, an excess of zeros, or a misspecified mean all inflate \(X^2\). Underdispersion, \(\hat\phi < 1\), also occurs, for counts bounded above for instance, and the negative binomial cannot represent it.

Weight of evidence centres on the sample

Weight of evidence asks a different contrast with the same fit. The sample default rate is \(100/700 = 0.1429\), and its logit is \(-1.7918\). A category’s weight of evidence is its own log-odds minus that overall logit.

The difference of the two weights equals the one-hot slope: \(\Delta\mathrm{WOE} = 2.9957 = \hat\beta_1\). Subtracting a constant does not change a variance, so the standard error of a weight of evidence equals the standard error of that category’s log-odds.

With a single categorical predictor the two codings describe one model. With several categorical predictors, Burakov notes that one-hot coefficients move when the reference level changes, while the weights of evidence stay centred on the overall event rate.

Overall default rate 100/700, logit \(-1.7918\). \(\Delta\mathrm{WOE}=2.9957=\hat\beta_1\). SE of WOE equals SE of category log-odds; with several factors, WOE stays centred when one-hot slopes move.

Softmax, drawn

The class probabilities sum to 1. The cross-entropy is \(-\sum_i\sum_k t_{ik}\log\pi_{ik}\), with \(t_{ik}\) the 1-of-\(K\) indicator.

Ordered categories are a cumulative model. Burakov notes them and stays with the unordered softmax.

A conformal interval uses a calibration set

The same chapter then builds an interval whose coverage is finite-sample, under exchangeability, from a calibration set that was not used to fit \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\).

  • Fit the logit on the training rows.

  • On the calibration rows, score each residual. The Pearson form he uses is \((y - \hat\pi)/\sqrt{\hat\pi(1-\hat\pi)}\).

  • Add and subtract a quantile of those scores. On the logit scale the interval is symmetric around \(\mathrm{logit}(\hat\pi)\), and the inverse logit brings it back to \((0,1)\) without clipping.

A classical conformal prediction set for a binary label is a set of classes. The interval here is for \(\pi\). Whether the 0/1 outcome falls inside a narrow band for \(\pi\) is a different question, and he treats it as the wrong coverage check.

Step three fragments: train fit; calibration Pearson scores; symmetric band on logit then inverse logit. Coverage is for \(\pi\), not for whether 0/1 falls in band—Burakov’s distinction on slide.

Going further. Split conformal prediction guarantees \(\Pr\{Y_{n+1} \in C(\mathbf{x}_{n+1})\} \geq 1-\alpha\) in finite samples when calibration and test points are exchangeable, using the \(\lceil (n_{\text{cal}}+1)(1-\alpha)\rceil\)-th smallest calibration score (Vovk, Gammerman and Shafer, Algorithmic Learning in a Random World; Lei and colleagues, 2018, Journal of the American Statistical Association). The guarantee is marginal, averaged over \(\mathbf{x}\); coverage conditional on a given \(\mathbf{x}\) cannot be guaranteed distribution-free (Foygel Barber and colleagues, 2021, Information and Inference). For a binary label the conformal object is a set of classes, \(\{0\}\), \(\{1\}\) or \(\{0,1\}\); Angelopoulos and Bates’s A Gentle Introduction to Conformal Prediction is the accessible entry.

Experimental design

🧮 Four blocks: contrasts in R, post-hoc tests and multiple testing, experimental designs, then mixed models in lme4. A short application closes each block. The worked answer is SPRUCE, except for the contrasts, which use CA-SYS.

1 · Contrasts in R

Treatment contrasts use one reference

Larmarange, chapter 26. For an unordered factor, R’s default is contr.treatment. A factor with \(n\) levels becomes \(n-1\) columns. The reference level sits in the intercept.

In the marker ~ grade example the intercept is \(1.0669\) and the grade II coefficient is \(-0.3864\). The mean at grade II is the sum:

\[ 1.0669 + (-0.3864) = 0.6805. \]

contr.treatment(n, base =) and contr.SAS() move which level is the reference.

Walk the arithmetic on the slide: intercept \(1.0669\) plus grade II coefficient \(-0.3864\) gives \(0.6805\). Emphasise \(n-1\) columns and one reference in the intercept. Students confuse “coefficient for II” with “mean at II” unless you do the sum aloud. contr.treatment and contr.SAS only move the reference level.

Going further. A factor with \(L\) levels and an intercept gives a cell-means model \(\mu_\ell\) with only \(L\) estimable means but \(L + 1\) parameters in the overparametrised form \(\beta_0 + \alpha_\ell\); a contrast coding is a choice of \(L - 1\) columns that removes the redundancy. The coding matrix \(\mathbf{C}\) (what contrasts() shows) is not the hypothesis matrix: the coefficients estimate the rows of the generalised inverse of \([\mathbf{1}\;\mathbf{C}]\), so reading a coefficient requires inverting the coding (Schad, Vasishth, Hohenstein and Kliegl, 2020, Journal of Memory and Language, “How to capitalize on a priori contrasts in linear (mixed) models: a tutorial”). With treatment coding the hypothesis matrix is simple, \(\beta_\ell = \mu_\ell - \mu_1\), which is why it reads well. In a model with an interaction, the “main effect” of another factor under treatment coding is its effect at the reference level only, a frequent misreading of type III tables. Any estimable contrast \(\sum_\ell c_\ell\mu_\ell\) with \(\sum_\ell c_\ell = 0\) can be obtained afterwards from any coding, for example with emmeans.

Sum contrasts use the mean of the level means

contr.sum compares each level with the unweighted mean of the level means. The last level is coded \(-1\), so one factor’s coefficients sum to zero and the intercept is that grand mean.

The grade level that was coded \(-1\) has deviation \(-(0.1525 - 0.2339) = 0.0814\), which is also \(0.9958 - 0.9144\).

Fitted values, residual sum of squares, and AIC match the treatment-contrast fit. What changes is the reading of each coefficient.

contr.sum centres on the unweighted mean of level means; the \(-1\) coding line explains the \(0.0814\) deviation. Stress that predictions do not move—only the sentences attached to each \(\hat\beta\). Ask which contrast you would use if the scientific question is “grade II versus average grade”.

Going further. Sum coding gives \(\beta_0 = \frac{1}{L}\sum_\ell \mu_\ell\) and \(\beta_\ell = \mu_\ell - \beta_0\) for \(\ell < L\), with the last deviation recovered as \(-\sum_{\ell<L}\beta_\ell\). The grand mean is unweighted, so with unequal group sizes it differs from the overall sample mean of \(Y\); a weighted-effect coding exists when the population mean is the target. Sum coding matters most with interactions: centred codings make the main effects in a factorial model average effects over the other factor’s levels, which is what type III sums of squares assume, whereas treatment coding makes them simple effects at a reference level. The two parametrisations span the same column space, so fitted values, residuals and likelihood are identical, exactly as the slide says; only the hypotheses tested by individual coefficients change.

An ordered factor can carry a trend

Further codings in the same chapter.

  • MASS::contr.sdif compares each level with the one before it. For grade, II minus I is \(-0.39\), the same gap as the treatment contrast against grade I.

  • contr.helmert compares each new level with the mean of the earlier levels. Keep it for a question that is exactly that comparison.

  • contr.poly is the default for an ordered factor. The columns are a linear, a quadratic, and a cubic trend. That is the coding for ordered time or dose when the question is the shape, including a bend. The intercept is again the mean of the level means.

Step three fragments in order: successive differences (contr.sdif), Helmert versus earlier mean, then polynomial trends for ordered dose or time. Tie contr.sdif’s \(-0.39\) back to the treatment contrast against grade I. Pick the coding to match the estimand, not R’s default habit.

Going further. contr.poly returns orthogonal polynomial contrasts: for \(L\) equally spaced levels, columns of degree \(1\) to \(L - 1\), each orthogonal to the others and to the intercept, scaled to unit length. With balanced data the linear, quadratic and cubic sums of squares then partition the factor’s sum of squares exactly, so a lack-of-fit test of linearity is the joint test of the degree-2-and-higher columns. The default assumes equal spacing; for unequally spaced doses pass the actual values, contr.poly(L, scores = ...), or the trend coefficients describe the wrong shape. Helmert contrasts are also mutually orthogonal under balance, but successive differences are not, so their coefficients are correlated. Because a coefficient’s meaning depends on scaling, report the fitted level means or the trend in units of \(x\) rather than the raw .L and .Q coefficients.

Eight minutes: which contrast? 📝

Pick one factor in your study, or system in CA-SYS, or warming in SPRUCE.

  • How many levels?
  • What is the reference, if there is one?
  • Is the question “each level against a baseline”, “each level against the mean”, or “the shape along an order”?

Eight minutes. The next slide is the CA-SYS reading. Do not hint at contr.sum until they have written a question in words.

One reading: CA-SYS systems

system has four levels, SD1, SD2, TS1, TS2. They are not an order.

  • Against a baseline, SD1 in the intercept: three coefficients, SD2, TS1, and TS2. That is contr.treatment
  • Against the mean of the four systems: contr.sum. The coefficients add to zero
  • Tillage, no-till against tilled, is a different contrast. It collapses SD1 with SD2, and TS1 with TS2. It is not one of the three system coefficients

Warming at SPRUCE is the ordered case: five steps, so a linear trend is the first column of contr.poly. The system factor is the one that needs a reference chosen on purpose.

Do the SD1 arithmetic only if someone asks. The point is that “the TS2 coefficient” is not “the mean at TS2” until you add the intercept. Mention the SPRUCE polynomial in one sentence and stop.

2 · Post-hoc tests and multiple testing

Contrasts from the model you fitted

When the groups and the covariates are in one model, the comparisons are contrasts from that fit. Heiss separates two averages. An average marginal effect averages the contrast over the observed rows. A marginal effect at the mean evaluates it at the average covariate. marginaleffects defaults to the first. emmeans defaults to the second. They differ when the model is not linear.

Reporting several of those contrasts is still a family. The adjustment is simultaneous inference for the family you planned, not a correction chosen after the significant rows appear.

Heiss: average marginal effect versus effect at mean; marginaleffects vs emmeans defaults. Several contrasts still form a family needing simultaneous inference.

Going further. For an inverse link \(h = g^{-1}\), the average marginal effect is \(n^{-1}\sum_i \partial h(\mathbf{x}_i^{\top}\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})/\partial x_1\) and the marginal effect at the mean is \(\partial h(\bar{\mathbf{x}}^{\top}\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})/\partial x_1\); by Jensen’s inequality they differ unless \(h\) is linear over the range of the data. Both are smooth functions of \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\), so their standard errors come from the delta method, which is what both packages compute. emmeans averages over a reference grid with equal weight per level, which is not the observed covariate distribution in an unbalanced design; say which grid you used. For a logit the derivative is \(\beta_1\pi(1-\pi)\), at most \(\beta_1/4\) at \(\pi = 1/2\): the divide-by-four rule of Gelman and Hill’s Data Analysis Using Regression and Multilevel/Hierarchical Models.

A row of coefficients is a family

\[ H_{0j}: \beta_j = 0, \quad j = 1, \ldots, p. \]

One row per coefficient hides that family. The matching statement is a joint region, or simultaneous intervals: Bonferroni intervals for a Bonferroni test, Tukey or Scheffé intervals for those contrast families. A logistic, Poisson, or negative-binomial model has the same family. The criterion does not change because the distribution did.

StatHarbor Analytics, Multiple Testing Correction (2026), from the slide “Multiplicity in Linear Models”. Testing and interval estimation are dual: a family-wise procedure induces simultaneous intervals with joint coverage at least \(1-\alpha\). Pointwise bands on a curve are the individual-test object; a simultaneous band is the corrected one.

Going further. Bonferroni controls the family-wise error rate at \(\alpha\) under any dependence, by the union bound; Holm’s step-down version (1979, Scandinavian Journal of Statistics) rejects at least as much with the same guarantee. Both are shortcuts of the closed-testing principle of Marcus, Peritz and Gabriel (1976, Biometrika): reject \(H_{0j}\) only when every intersection hypothesis that contains it is rejected at level \(\alpha\). For the coefficients of one fitted model, \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\) is approximately multivariate normal, so the exact critical value is a quantile of the maximum of correlated \(|z|\) statistics; Hothorn, Bretz and Westfall (2008, Biometrical Journal) implement this in multcomp::glht for lm, glm and mixed models alike (Bretz et al. 2016).

The follow-up matches the family

After a global analysis of variance, name the contrasts before you test them.

  • All pairwise means: Tukey.

  • Each treatment against a control: Dunnett.

  • Arbitrary contrasts: Scheffé, or simultaneous inference from the fitted model.

The correction belongs to that family. It is not a fee paid because several means exist.

Tukey all pairs, Dunnett versus control, Scheffé arbitrary—match procedure to planned family. Correction is not a tariff for having many means.

Going further. Tukey’s procedure uses the studentised range, the law of the largest standardised difference among \(K\) means, and is exact for a balanced design with equal variances; the Tukey–Kramer version for unequal group sizes is conservative. Dunnett’s uses the joint multivariate-\(t\) law of the \(K-1\) comparisons with the control, which share the control mean and are positively correlated, so its critical value is smaller than Tukey’s. Scheffé’s critical value, \(\sqrt{(K-1)F_{K-1,\nu}(1-\alpha)}\) with \(\nu\) residual degrees of freedom, covers every contrast at once, including those chosen after looking, and is therefore the widest. All three are cases of simultaneous inference on linear functions of \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\) (Bretz et al. 2016).

Genomics is a large exploratory family

A screen of thousands of genes, tens of thousands of proteins, or millions of variants is a different family. Missing a true signal is costly, and a controlled share of false leads is acceptable.

That is a false-discovery rate: Benjamini–Hochberg, an adaptive version, or a \(q\)-value. A \(q\)-value is not a posterior probability that the finding is true. A family-wise guarantee of no false claim at all spends power the screen cannot afford.

Thousands of features: FDR (BH, adaptive, \(q\)-value) not FWER. \(q\) is not posterior probability of truth—power trade-off on slide.

Going further. With \(V\) false rejections among \(R\), the false-discovery rate is \(\mathbb{E}\{V/\max(R,1)\}\). Benjamini and Hochberg (1995, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B) sort the \(m\) \(p\)-values and reject the \(k\) smallest, for the largest \(k\) with \(p_{(k)} \leq k\alpha/m\); this controls the rate at \(m_0\alpha/m \leq \alpha\) under independence and under positive regression dependence (Benjamini and Yekutieli, 2001, Annals of Statistics), and under any dependence if \(\alpha\) is divided by \(\sum_{k=1}^{m} 1/k\). Adaptive versions estimate the null proportion \(m_0/m\) and gain power when many features are non-null. Storey’s \(q\)-value (2003, Annals of Statistics) is the smallest false-discovery rate at which a feature would be called: a property of a list, not of one feature (Farcomeni 2008).

One false claim, or some false signal

  • A family-wise error rate is the right target when even one false claim is costly.

  • A false-discovery rate is the right target when the aim is broad discovery and some controlled false signal is acceptable.

  • Dependence, a hierarchy, or a structured set of contrasts often recovers power that a generic worst-case correction spends.

A procedure that controls the family-wise rate also controls the false-discovery rate, usually at that cost in power.

Because \(V \le R\) whenever \(R > 0\), the false-discovery rate is at most the family-wise error rate. Holm rejects every hypothesis Bonferroni rejects, for the same family and the same level. Questions before choosing: what is the family, is the setting confirmatory or exploratory, what false-positive burden is tolerable, and are the tests independent, positively dependent, or structured? Report the family, the criterion, the procedure, and the adjusted summary. Do not choose the correction after seeing which rows were small.

Which procedure for which family

Scenario Family Typical procedure
Primary confirmatory endpoints Small and prespecified Holm, gatekeeping, closed testing
All pairwise means Structured contrasts Tukey HSD
Many genomic features Very large, exploratory Benjamini–Hochberg, adaptive BH, \(q\)-values
Complex dependence Structured and correlated Westfall–Young, or a bootstrap calibration

Define the family and the error criterion before the claims. This grid is from StatHarbor Analytics, Multiple Testing Correction (2026).

Walk the table: confirmatory Holm/gatekeeping; pairwise Tukey; genomics BH; dependence Westfall–Young or bootstrap. StatHarbor 2026 grid—define family before claims.

Two places to go next

(Bretz et al. 2016) develops these procedures as maximum statistics and shows the R implementations. (Farcomeni 2008) reviews the false-discovery proportion, dependence among the statistics, and the genomic case.

Bretz multiple comparisons book for R implementations; Farcomeni review for FDR and dependence. Bibliography slide—thirty seconds unless someone asks for a recommendation.

3 · Experimental designs

The analysis inherits the plan

A mixed model does not repair an undescribed design. Before the formula, name:

  • the unit that received the treatment
  • the unit that was measured
  • what was randomised, blocked, or only observed
  • which rows are repeats of the same unit

Carbon data are often hierarchical, multi-site, and repeated in time.

Open with the headline: the formula cannot fix a plan you never wrote down. Walk the four bullets in order and ask the room to name SPRUCE’s treatment unit (the enclosure) and the observational unit on a flux row (collar by date). The common slip is to treat every depth–date line as an independent replicate; that mistake is what the random effect is meant to encode, not to paper over.

Going further. Hurlbert (1984, Ecological Monographs, “Pseudoreplication and the design of ecological field experiments”) named the error: testing a treatment effect with an error term built from samples that are not independent replicates of the treatment. His taxonomy separates simple pseudoreplication (one unit per treatment, many samples from it), temporal pseudoreplication (repeated dates treated as replicates), and sacrificial pseudoreplication (real replicates pooled before the test). The formal statement is that the correct denominator for a treatment comparison is the variance between experimental units, the stratum in which the treatment was randomised; a mixed model recovers it only if the random-effect structure matches that stratum. Bailey, Design of Comparative Experiments (2008), makes the distinction between experimental unit and observational unit the starting point of every analysis.

A study leaves some conditions free

In a study, conditions that move the outcome are outside the investigator’s control. A field example is the weather, the food, and the predators.

  • In an observational study the variable of interest itself is not assigned. That is where the reminder sits: correlation is not causation.

Field weather is the uncontrolled nuisance example. Step the fragment: the exposure of interest is not assigned, so the causal section’s \(do(x)\) language matters later. SPRUCE is not this slide—it is closer to the controlled-experiment and trial pair.

A trial randomises the assignment

A randomised controlled trial still cannot hold every nuisance fixed. It does control who receives the intervention.

  • With a large enough sample, the nuisances average out, and the contrast can be read as an effect of that assignment.

  • The trial is prospective: the outcome is unknown when the groups are assigned.

Fragment one: randomisation controls assignment, not every nuisance. Fragment two: prospective timing—outcome unknown at allocation. Ask whether warming at SPRUCE is “assigned” in this sense (yes on enclosure). Bridge to the causal deck: randomisation is a design fact, not a covariate trick.

Going further. In potential-outcome notation, each unit has \(Y_i(1)\) and \(Y_i(0)\), and randomisation makes the assignment independent of both, so the difference of group means is unbiased for the average treatment effect without any model for the nuisances. “Average out” is a statement about the randomisation distribution, not about one realised allocation: a given trial can still be imbalanced on a covariate, and adjusting for a pre-specified prognostic covariate then gains precision without bias (Senn, 1994, Statistics in Medicine, “Testing for baseline balance in clinical trials”, argues against testing for imbalance instead). Fisher’s randomisation test uses the assignment mechanism itself as the reference distribution, so its validity needs no normality or independence assumption beyond the design. Imbens and Rubin, Causal Inference for Statistics, Social, and Biomedical Sciences (2015), chapters 5–7, develop the finite-population theory.

A meta-analysis studies the studies

Huber calls a meta-analysis an observational study of earlier experiments or studies. Two motives: a larger effective sample, and the hope that study-level bias averages out across studies.

The hierarchical version, one estimate per site, is fixed effect or random effects.

Meta-analysis is observational at study level: you did not randomise which papers exist. The two motives on the slide are sample size and hope that study-level bias averages out—say both, without overselling the second. Point to the link back to fixed versus random effects for “one estimate per site”.

Going further. With study estimates \(\hat\theta_j\) and within-study variances \(v_j\), the fixed-effect (common-effect) estimate is the inverse-variance mean \(\sum_j w_j\hat\theta_j / \sum_j w_j\) with \(w_j = 1/v_j\); the random-effects model adds \(\theta_j \sim \mathcal{N}(\theta, \tau^2)\) and uses \(w_j = 1/(v_j + \tau^2)\), which flattens the weights and widens the interval. DerSimonian and Laird (1986, Controlled Clinical Trials, “Meta-analysis in clinical trials”) give the moment estimator of \(\tau^2\); REML or Paule–Mandel estimators and the Hartung–Knapp–Sidik–Jonkman interval behave better when the number of studies is small. \(I^2\) describes the share of variability due to heterogeneity, not its size. Borenstein, Hedges, Higgins and Rothstein, Introduction to Meta-Analysis (2009), is the standard text.

Randomise the nuisance you cannot block

When the nuisance is unknown in advance, randomisation is the practical strategy: at a large enough sample, its effect averages out. It also limits unconscious bias, such as extra care for the samples that were hard to obtain.

He points to Senn (2004) for the ways a “better” scheme than simple randomisation can go wrong.

When blocking is impossible, randomisation is the practical defence—both against unknown nuisances and unconscious handling bias. Mention Senn as the caution on fancy schemes without lecturing the chapter. Ask for one carbon-lab nuisance you could randomise but not block (plate position, run order).

Going further. Randomisation does two separate jobs. It removes systematic bias, because any unmeasured covariate is independent of treatment in expectation; and it justifies the error term, because under the randomisation the expected treatment mean square equals the residual mean square when there is no effect (Fisher, The Design of Experiments, 1935). Restricted randomisation (blocking, stratification, minimisation) keeps both properties only if the analysis includes the restriction, which is why a blocked design must have the block in the model. Run order and plate position are classic carriers of drift; a randomised order turns drift into noise, while a systematic order turns it into bias. Senn’s 2004 discussion of “better” allocation schemes (Statistics in Medicine) makes the point that deterministic balancing can break the link between design and analysis.

Balance makes each effect identifiable

A balanced design gives every factor combination the same number of replicates. Each factor’s effect can then be separated. A nuisance that is balanced against the factor of interest is in the same position.

  • An unbalanced plan can be forced by cost. The warning is that the analysis is then on thin ice.

Balanced means equal replication per combination so effects separate. Step the fragment: unbalanced designs are common when money runs out—keep the “thin ice” phrase for the methods section. Do not confuse balance with randomisation; you need both stories in different papers.

Going further. In a linear model \(\mathbb{E}(\mathbf{Y}) = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta\), a linear function \(\mathbf{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol\beta\) is estimable when \(\mathbf{c}^{\top}\) lies in the row space of \(\mathbf{X}\); an empty cell, as in the right-hand grid, makes the corresponding interaction non-estimable. With equal replication the columns for different factors are orthogonal, so the sums of squares decompose uniquely and the order of terms does not matter. Unbalanced data break that orthogonality: sequential (type I), partial (type II) and marginal (type III) sums of squares then test different hypotheses, and type III tests on main effects in the presence of an interaction depend on the contrast coding. Searle, Linear Models for Unbalanced Data (1987), is the reference; Agresti covers estimability in Foundations of Linear and Generalized Linear Models (Agresti 2015).

Two questions for every factor

📄 Krzywinski, Altman and Blainey, Nested designs, Nature Methods (2014). Their one-line advice: when the noise comes from several levels, analyse the experiment as a nested design.

  • Crossed or nested: crossed when every level of one factor meets every level of the other; nested when each lower level belongs to one upper level, as mouse 3 only ever sits under drug 2
  • Fixed or random: fixed when you chose the levels to compare them and would use them again, such as a drug or a dose; random when the levels are a sample, such as mice or cells, and the target is their variance

A fixed factor is compared against the variance of the level it was applied to.

Two questions, asked of every factor before any formula. Use the drug–mouse–cell example of the next slide: drug is fixed, mouse and cell are random; mice are nested in drug when each mouse receives one drug. The last sentence is the practical one: a drug given to whole mice is compared with mouse-to-mouse variation, not with cell-to-cell variation. That is pseudoreplication seen from the design side.

The paper itself is behind a paywall; the slide uses only its standfirst and its figure of crossed and nested factors, redrawn on the next slide.

Going further. In a balanced two-level nested design with \(a\) drugs, \(b\) mice per drug and \(n\) cells per mouse, the expected mean squares are \(\mathbb{E}(\mathrm{MS}_{\text{drug}}) = \sigma_\varepsilon^2 + n\sigma_{\text{mouse}}^2 + bn\,\theta_{\text{drug}}^2\) and \(\mathbb{E}(\mathrm{MS}_{\text{mouse(drug)}}) = \sigma_\varepsilon^2 + n\sigma_{\text{mouse}}^2\).
