The drug \(F\) ratio is therefore \(\mathrm{MS}_{\text{drug}}/\mathrm{MS}_{\text{mouse(drug)}}\) on \(a-1\) and \(a(b-1)\) degrees of freedom: more cells per mouse shrink \(\sigma_\varepsilon^2/n\) but leave the mouse term, so the number of mice drives the power. Montgomery, Design and Analysis of Experiments, chapter 14, gives the derivation.

Four ways to arrange drug, mouse and cell

Colour marks a fixed factor, grey a random one. from “Factors may be crossed or nested” in Krzywinski, Altman and Blainey (2014).

Walk the four panels left to right, top to bottom. a: three fixed factors, every combination present, a factorial; no random term at all. b: each mouse receives one drug and each cell belongs to one mouse—the drug comparison has as many replicates as mice. c: each mouse receives both drugs, so the mouse acts as a block and the drug contrast is made inside each mouse. d: tissues nested in mice, cells nested in tissues, and the drug assigned to cells, so drug is crossed with the hierarchy at the bottom. Ask where SPRUCE sits: panel b, with enclosure for mouse and warming for drug.

The original is a small published figure; it is redrawn here because the copy available was too small to read. In the original, tissue is a fixed factor (two named tissues compared); that is why it is coloured.

Crossed, nested, blocked, split

Schielzeth and Nakagawa, Figure 1. Solid lines are a partial cross. Dashed lines complete it. The SPRUCE reading of the same picture is crossed, nested, or both. 📄 The paper.

Four panels: crossed, nested, randomised block, split-plot. Point to solid versus dashed lines in the caption—partial versus completed cross. Map split-plot to large-unit versus within-unit factors without re-deriving the cookie-dough story. [#sec-crossed-nested], in the mixed-model block, puts the SPRUCE labels on the same picture.

A short map of plans

Plan What is randomised or assigned
Completely randomised Treatments to units, with no blocking factor
Randomised block Treatments inside a block that soaks up a nuisance gradient
Factorial Two or more factors crossed, so that interactions exist
Split-plot or strip-plot A hard-to-change factor on the large unit, another factor inside it
Regression or gradient A continuous driver, with enough levels to see the shape
Nested or hierarchical Units inside units, when crossing is impossible

Tanaka’s edibble slides are a precise way to write units and treatments down before you fit anything.

Use the table as a menu, not a checklist. Pause on split-plot: the hard-to-change factor is randomised on the large unit (enclosure \(\mathrm{CO}_2\)), while the easy factor can sit inside (collar schedule). Ask which row best describes CA-SYS tillage zones versus the mixed zone. Tanaka is the homework link for writing units before lmer().

Going further. A split-plot has two randomisations and therefore two error strata. With \(a\) whole-plot levels in \(r\) blocks and \(b\) subplot levels, the whole-plot factor \(A\) is tested against the whole-plot error (block \(\times\) \(A\), \((r-1)(a-1)\) degrees of freedom), while the subplot factor \(B\) and the \(A \times B\) interaction are tested against the smaller subplot error, \(a(r-1)(b-1)\) degrees of freedom. The design deliberately buys precision for \(B\) and \(A \times B\) at the expense of \(A\); analysing it as a factorial with one residual overstates the evidence for \(A\). In a mixed model, the whole-plot error is the random effect (1 | block:A), and with balanced data REML reproduces the stratified ANOVA exactly. Yates (1937) introduced the split-plot analysis; Bailey, Design of Comparative Experiments (2008), and Montgomery, Design and Analysis of Experiments, chapter 14, give the expected mean squares.

Do not bin the gradient you built

SPRUCE kept five warming levels, \(+0\) to \(+9^\circ\mathrm{C}\) in steps of \(2.25^\circ\mathrm{C}\), each at ambient and elevated CO\(_2\), on ten enclosures.

A regression on that gradient was the design. Splitting it into “low” and “high” spends the shape the levels were built to show. The number of enclosures still has to exceed the number of parameters.

This is the slide the pitfalls section points at. Five levels are a regression, not a two-group test. Ten enclosures cannot carry a saturated \(5 \times 2\) cell-means model with a residual. One minute.

Going further. For a straight-line model, \(\mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta_1) = \sigma^2 / \sum_i (x_i - \bar x)^2\), so the slope uses every level’s distance from the mean; binning replaces \(x\) by a group indicator and, for a linear truth with evenly spread levels, loses a substantial share of that information (Cohen, 1983, Applied Psychological Measurement, “The cost of dichotomization”, shows that a median split of a normal \(x\) costs the equivalent of about 38% of the sample). The variance formula also says the D-optimal design for a known straight line puts half the units at each extreme; SPRUCE’s five equally spaced levels are a deliberate compromise that keeps the power to detect curvature. Ten enclosures leave \(10 - p\) residual degrees of freedom: intercept, slope, \(\mathrm{CO}_2\), and their product leave six, a saturated \(5 \times 2\) means model leaves none.

Ten minutes: name the units 📝

On your own study, or on SPRUCE or CA-SYS, write four lines:

  • the unit that received the treatment, or the exposure
  • the unit that was measured
  • what was assigned, blocked, or only observed
  • which rows are repeats of the same unit

Ten minutes, writing, not talking. If a group has no study of their own, send them to SPRUCE. Do not show the next slide until the time is up.

One reading: SPRUCE

SPRUCE is the designed case, so the words are easier to pin down than in an observational table.

  • Treatment unit: the enclosure. Warming and CO\(_2\) are assigned there
  • Measured unit: a depth on a date, inside that enclosure
  • Assigned: the ten chambered enclosures. Two ambient plots were never given a warming level
  • Repeats: depths and dates that share an enclosure are not new enclosures
If you need… The replicate is…
The warming slope The enclosure, \(n = 10\)
A collar method Collars within an enclosure
A seasonal curve Dates within an enclosure

Read the four bullets, then the table. \(n = 10\) is the line that surprises people who counted depth-date rows. Offer CA-SYS only if a group chose it: plot is \(j\), point is \(i\).

4 · Mixed models

Each layout names its random terms

The design decides which factors get a random intercept. The lowest random level, the cell, is the residual \(\varepsilon\).

Layout Random factors Independent unit Random part in lme4
a Crossed none each culture in the grid none: lm()
b Nested mouse, cell the mouse (1 | mouse)
c Crossed and nested mouse, cell the mouse (1 | mouse), and (1 | mouse:drug) with several cells per mouse and drug
d Nested and crossed mouse, cell the mouse (1 | mouse/tissue), with tissue fixed or random

SPRUCE is layout b with one more level: warming for drug, enclosure for mouse, collar inside the enclosure, and dates as the cells.

Read the “independent unit” column first: in b, c and d it is the mouse, whatever the number of cells. That column is the outer plate of the diagrams that follow. Then the formula column. Layout c is the one people under-specify: if each mouse has several cells under each drug, the drug effect can vary between mice, and (1 | mouse:drug) is that variance; without it the drug test uses the cell-level residual and is too optimistic.

Going further. With \(m\) rows per cluster and intraclass correlation \(\rho = \sigma_u^2/(\sigma_u^2 + \sigma_\varepsilon^2)\), the variance of a mean over \(J\) clusters is inflated by the design effect \(1 + (m - 1)\rho\) relative to \(Jm\) independent rows (Kish, Survey Sampling, 1965). The effective sample size is \(Jm / \big(1 + (m-1)\rho\big)\), which tends to \(J/\rho\) as \(m\) grows: adding cells to a mouse cannot buy more information than the mice themselves carry. Even \(\rho = 0.1\) with \(m = 21\) triples the variance. For a treatment assigned to clusters, as in layout b, the test has of the order of \(J\) minus the number of cluster-level parameters degrees of freedom, not \(Jm\).

Crossed, nested, or both

Warming and \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) are crossed on the enclosure. Collars and dates are nested in the enclosure: each inner plate repeats inside the outer one. A technical replicate nested in a core is a further level, and it is rarely the level of inference.

Read the plates from the outside in: warming and \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) are constants on enclosure \(j\); collar \(k\) and date \(i\) are nested inside. Ask where a core technical replicate would hang, and whether inference should live there. Schielzeth Figure 1, in the design block, is the same vocabulary with different ink; layout b of the drug–mouse–cell figure is the same shape.

A random intercept is a distribution on \(u_j\)

Use a Gaussian equation for \(Y_{ij}\) only when \(Y\) can live on that scale. For a count or a detection, the cluster term sits on the link, as in the diagram. Only the outer plate counts as independent replication.

\(u_j\) is a property of the cluster. It is not a covariate you forgot to measure, unless you are willing to say so. Ignoring it is the pitfall repeated rows are not replicates.

Read the plates: \(u_j\) is drawn once per independent unit, and every replicate \(i\) inside that unit shares it. The equation is on the link scale, not on the count scale unless \(Y\) is Gaussian. \(u_j \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_u^2)\) is a distribution over enclosures, not a missing fixed covariate. If someone proposes “just add enclosure as a factor”, ask whether they have all levels or a sample of bogs—that leads into the next slide’s columns.

Going further. For a Gaussian \(Y\), the random intercept induces a compound-symmetric covariance within a cluster: \(\mathrm{Var}(Y_{ij}) = \sigma_u^2 + \sigma_\varepsilon^2\) and \(\mathrm{Cov}(Y_{ij}, Y_{i'j}) = \sigma_u^2\), so the intraclass correlation is \(\rho = \sigma_u^2/(\sigma_u^2 + \sigma_\varepsilon^2)\). On a non-identity link the story changes: \(\beta_1\) in a generalised linear mixed model is a conditional (cluster-specific) effect, and the marginal, population-averaged effect is attenuated; for a logit link, roughly \(\beta_1/\sqrt{1 + 0.346\,\sigma_u^2}\) (Zeger, Liang and Albert, 1988, Biometrics). The likelihood integrates over \(u_j\), which has no closed form for non-Gaussian \(Y\); Laplace approximation (glmer() default) or adaptive Gauss–Hermite quadrature (nAGQ > 1) is needed, and both are less accurate with few observations per cluster. Testing \(\sigma_u^2 = 0\) puts the null on the boundary of the parameter space, so the likelihood-ratio statistic follows a 50:50 mixture of \(\chi^2_0\) and \(\chi^2_1\), not \(\chi^2_1\) (Self and Liang, 1987, Journal of the American Statistical Association).

Fixed and random name the target

Fixed

A contrast you want to report, such as the warming slope.

If you already have every level in the population, a fixed indicator for each level is coherent.

Random

A level you want to generalise over, such as enclosures drawn from a bog.

Ten enclosures is a small sample of a variance. \(\hat\sigma_u\) will be noisy.

Partial pooling is the practical reason to bother: an enclosure with two bad weeks borrows strength from the others. The meta-analysis version, one estimate per site, is fixed effect or random effects.

Left column: warming slope is a fixed estimand you report. Right column: enclosures are a random draw from a bog population, and ten of them makes \(\hat\sigma_u\) noisy—quote that line. Partial pooling is the punchline for sparse clusters. The meta-analysis slide, earlier in the hour, is the same idea with one estimate per site.

Going further. In the balanced Gaussian random-intercept model, the predicted cluster effect (the BLUP) is \(\hat u_j = \lambda_j(\bar Y_{\cdot j} - \hat\mu)\) with shrinkage factor \(\lambda_j = \sigma_u^2/(\sigma_u^2 + \sigma_\varepsilon^2/m_j)\): a cluster with few rows or noisy rows is pulled harder towards the grand mean. That is partial pooling between the two extremes, no pooling (a fixed effect per cluster, \(\lambda_j = 1\)) and complete pooling (ignore clusters, \(\lambda_j = 0\)). Robinson (1991, Statistical Science, “That BLUP is a good thing: the estimation of random effects”) reviews the theory, and Gelman and Hill, Data Analysis Using Regression and Multilevel/Hierarchical Models (2007), chapter 12, gives the applied reading. With ten clusters \(\hat\sigma_u^2\) is imprecise and can be estimated as zero, a singular fit, in which case the model reduces silently to complete pooling.

Nesting is a property of the experiment

Schielzeth and Nakagawa (Methods in Ecology and Evolution, 2013). A nested factor can be fitted with the syntax of a crossed factor, provided each nested level has a unique label. The design still decides what the variances mean.

The difference that matters is the interaction variance. In a nested experiment it is pooled with the main-effect variance of the nested factor. A crossed experiment can separate the two. The pooling is fixed by which combinations occur, not by the formula.

If a cross would have been feasible and meaningful, the data are nested by design, and the pooling has to be stated. If a cross would be irrelevant, the nesting is natural.

Schielzeth and Nakagawa: unique labels let nested factors use crossed syntax, but the experiment still decides what variances mean. The interaction variance pools with the nested main effect in a nested design; a cross can separate them. Ask whether enclosure-by-collar should be crossed or nested given how SPRUCE was built—the plate diagram earlier in this block is the answer key.

Going further. In a balanced two-way random model with \(a\) levels of \(A\), \(b\) of \(B\) and \(n\) replicates per cell, the expected mean squares are \(\mathbb{E}(\mathrm{MS}_A) = \sigma_\varepsilon^2 + n\sigma_{AB}^2 + bn\sigma_A^2\) and \(\mathbb{E}(\mathrm{MS}_{AB}) = \sigma_\varepsilon^2 + n\sigma_{AB}^2\), so \(\sigma_A^2\) is separable from \(\sigma_{AB}^2\) only because \(B\) is crossed with \(A\). If \(B\) is nested in \(A\), the corresponding mean square estimates \(\sigma_\varepsilon^2 + n(\sigma_{B}^2 + \sigma_{AB}^2)\): the two variances are confounded, which is the pooling Schielzeth and Nakagawa describe. In lme4 syntax, (1 | A/B) expands to (1 | A) + (1 | A:B), and (1 | A) + (1 | B) with uniquely labelled \(B\) levels fits the same model; the syntax cannot recover a variance the design never separated. Searle, Casella and McCulloch, Variance Components (1992), give the full derivations.

Four variances, if the design allows them

A crossed design can estimate each of those four variances. Nested sampling leaves the interaction inside the nested factor’s variance.

Figure 2 flows from two factors and their interaction into trait value, then down to four variance components. In a cross you can estimate interaction variance separately; nested sampling pools it. Students often fit (1|nested) and interpret \(\sigma_u^2\) as “noise” without stating what was pooled.

The four layouts in lme4

One formula per panel. The data frames are placeholders; the point is which term each design needs.

layouts.R

library(lme4)
# a  crossed and all fixed: a factorial, no random term
lm(y ~ drug * dose * diet, data = d_a)
# b  drug given to whole mice, cells inside mice
lmer(y ~ drug + (1 | mouse), data = d_b)
# c  every mouse receives both drugs
lmer(y ~ drug + (1 | mouse) + (1 | mouse:drug), data = d_c)
# d  tissues inside mice, drug assigned to cells within a tissue
lmer(y ~ drug + (1 | mouse/tissue), data = d_d)

In b, give each mouse a unique label: mouse 1 under drug 2 is not mouse 1 under drug 1. lmerTest::lmer() adds Satterthwaite tests; in b the drug test has about the number of mice minus two degrees of freedom.

Read the four calls against the panels. a has no random term because every factor is fixed. b: the drug is a mouse-level covariate, so its standard error is driven by the mouse variance. c: the mouse is a block; the drug contrast is within mouse. d: (1 | mouse/tissue) expands to (1 | mouse) + (1 | mouse:tissue); drug varies within tissue, so it is tested against the cell-level residual, and (drug | mouse) would let the drug effect vary between mice.

The unique-label point is the most common coding error: with labels 1–2 reused under each drug, (1 | mouse) silently crosses mice with drug. Either relabel, or write (1 | drug:mouse).

Going further. In balanced nested data, REML reproduces the classical nested ANOVA: the estimated mouse variance is \((\mathrm{MS}_{\text{mouse(drug)}} - \mathrm{MS}_\varepsilon)/n\), truncated at zero, and the Satterthwaite degrees of freedom for drug equal \(a(b-1)\), the mouse-within-drug count. With unbalanced data the two diverge, and Kenward–Roger (pbkrtest) is the safer small-sample choice. A zero variance estimate gives a singular fit; lme4 warns, and the model then collapses to complete pooling for that level (Bates, Mächler, Bolker and Walker, Journal of Statistical Software, 2015).

ML and REML answer different targets

The practical gap is often small. A likelihood-ratio comparison of two models uses ML.

Question ML REML
Fixed part of the model ✅ More accurate for the fixed part Usable, and usually close
Variance components Usable, and usually close ✅ More accurate for the random variances
Comparing two models ✅ Required for a likelihood-ratio test Switch to ML before the comparison
On a typical fit Often close to REML The usual reporting fit
Angelino and Marcone, September 2026. Their general wisdom on ML and REML.

Use the rendered table: ML for comparing nested models by likelihood ratio; REML for variance components on a typical report. The row “Comparing two models” is the one students forget—switch to ML before the LRT. Angelino and Marcone are the source note at the bottom of the table.

Going further. For a Gaussian linear model with \(p\) fixed effects, ML gives \(\hat\sigma^2 = \mathrm{RSS}/n\), biased downward by the factor \((n - p)/n\) because it ignores the degrees of freedom spent on \(\boldsymbol\beta\); REML maximises the likelihood of \(n - p\) error contrasts \(\mathbf{K}^{\top}\mathbf{Y}\) with \(\mathbf{K}^{\top}\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{0}\), which do not depend on \(\boldsymbol\beta\), and recovers \(\mathrm{RSS}/(n - p)\) (Patterson and Thompson, 1971, Biometrika). In mixed models the same correction matters most when the number of clusters is small relative to the cluster-level fixed effects, exactly the SPRUCE case. Because the REML likelihood depends on \(\mathbf{X}\), two REML fits with different fixed effects are likelihoods of different data, so their ratio is meaningless; two REML fits with the same fixed part and different random parts can be compared. Harville (1977, Journal of the American Statistical Association) also gives the Bayesian reading: REML is the marginal likelihood after integrating \(\boldsymbol\beta\) out under a flat prior.

nlme carries the residual correlation

The same course names two R packages. nlme is the one they single out for a flexible covariance. lme4 is the other. The split below is what the two fitting functions actually expose.

Question nlme::lme lme4::lmer
Residual correlation in time ✅ correlation =, including corAR1() No correlation argument on lmer()
Likelihood method = "REML" or "ML" ✅ REML = TRUE by default
More than one cluster One random formula is the natural case ✅ Several (1 | group) terms in one formula

Read the three rows: nlme::lme exposes correlation =, including corAR1(); lmer() does not take a correlation argument on the residual. lme4 wins on multiple (1|group) terms in one formula. Pick the package to match whether residual time correlation or multiple clusters is the harder problem.

Going further. Neither package gives exact \(F\) tests for fixed effects in unbalanced mixed models, because the null distribution of the Wald statistic depends on estimated variance components. nlme reports \(t\) and \(F\) with “containment” denominator degrees of freedom taken from the grouping level where each term varies; lmer() reports no \(P\) values at all. lmerTest adds the Satterthwaite approximation, which matches the first two moments of the variance of \(\mathbf{c}^{\top}\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\) to a scaled \(\chi^2\), and pbkrtest the Kenward–Roger method (Kenward and Roger, 1997, Biometrics), which also inflates the covariance matrix of \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\) for the uncertainty in the variance components and is the more accurate choice with few clusters. With ten enclosures, both give denominator degrees of freedom near the enclosure-level count, not the number of rows; a parametric bootstrap of the likelihood ratio is the alternative when the approximations are in doubt. The AR(1) term in nlme models \(\mathrm{Cor}(\varepsilon_{ij}, \varepsilon_{i'j}) = \phi^{|t_i - t_{i'}|}\) within a cluster (Pinheiro and Bates, Mixed-Effects Models in S and S-PLUS, 2000, chapter 5).

Eight minutes: where does \(u_j\) sit? 📝

On your hierarchy, or on SPRUCE:

  • what is \(j\), and what is \(i\)?
  • which factor is fixed, because you would use those levels again?
  • which factor is random, because the levels are a sample you want to generalise?

Eight minutes. The answer slide is SPRUCE, because the enclosure is a sample of a bog and the warming levels are the ones the design would use again.

One reading: an enclosure effect

  • \(j\) is the enclosure. \(i\) is a depth, or a date, inside it
  • Warming and CO\(_2\) are fixed. Those levels are the contrast
  • The enclosure is random if the target is a bog, not these ten boxes alone. Ten levels is a small sample of \(\sigma_u^2\)
  • \(u_j\) sits on the link. Depths that share an enclosure share that draw

A model that ignores \(j\) treats two depths in one enclosure as if they were two enclosures. That is the interval that is too small.

Write \(u_j\) on the link, not on the copy-number scale, unless they are already on \(\log_{10}\). Ten enclosures means \(\hat\sigma_u\) will be noisy. Say that, then stop. The longitudinal random-slope picture is in the file and hidden.

Going further. Power for a cluster-level treatment depends on the number of clusters far more than on rows per cluster: for a two-arm comparison with \(J\) clusters per arm and \(m\) rows each, the standard error of the difference is \(\sqrt{2(\sigma_u^2 + \sigma_\varepsilon^2/m)/J}\), which hits a floor of \(\sqrt{2\sigma_u^2/J}\) however large \(m\) becomes. The required number of clusters is the individually randomised sample size times the design effect \(1 + (m-1)\rho\), divided by \(m\), plus a small-sample correction because the test has about \(2J - 2\) degrees of freedom (Donner and Klar, Design and Analysis of Cluster Randomization Trials in Health Research, 2000). For complex designs, simulate: generate data from the fitted mixed model with the planned \(J\), \(m\) and effect size, refit, and count rejections, for example with the simr package (Green and MacLeod, 2016, Methods in Ecology and Evolution). With ten enclosures, the useful planning question is the smallest warming slope detectable with reasonable power, not whether more depths would help.

Repeated measures are a time series inside \(j\)

Do not run a separate test at each date and then narrate the dates that were “significant”.

A first model for a repeated flux:

  • a term for time, or for season
  • the treatment, which does not change inside the enclosure
  • the treatment \(\times\) time interaction, if the contrast itself changes
  • a dependence for the residuals, or a random intercept for the enclosure

Dates are \(i\). They do not become new experimental units because there are many of them.

Warn against the “significant Tuesdays” narrative first. Then walk the bullet list: treatment is constant inside enclosure \(j\); interaction matters if warming changes the time course. Index \(i\) is the wave, not a new experimental unit. This slide sets up the AR(1) and (time | enclosure) calls near the end of the section.

Repeated in time is longitudinal

Angelino and Marcone, September 2026: a repeated-measures design records each individual more than once. The design is longitudinal when those repeats are ordered in time.

Three predictors sit beside \(Y\): time, a covariate that changes with time, and a covariate that does not. The aim is how \(\mu\) depends on them across the waves.

Godechot’s panel is the econometric name for the same layout: several dates for one person, set against a single cross-section. Within-person changes become visible, and age can be separated from cohort.

Angelino and Marcone: repeated measures becomes longitudinal when time is ordered. Name the three predictor types beside \(Y\)—time, time-varying covariate, time-invariant covariate. Godechot’s panel vocabulary helps economists in the room; enclosure waves are the carbon analogue.

Classical repeated-measures ANOVA wants a rectangle

The same course lists two limits. The ANOVA keeps only people with every wave. It also assumes sphericity: every pair of times has the same variance of the difference. When that fails, the \(F\) ratios inflate.

A mixed model keeps an incomplete person. The dependence goes into \(u_j\), or into a residual correlation. Dates stay index \(i\). They do not become new experimental units.

Two limits of classical RM-ANOVA: complete cases only, and sphericity of differenced times. When sphericity fails, \(F\) ratios inflate. Mixed models keep partial follow-up and put dependence in \(u_j\) or correlated residuals—preview corAR1 on the nlme slide. Dates remain index \(i\), not new units.

The line is allowed to vary inside \(j\)

Model

\[ Y_{ij} = (\beta_0 + u_{0j}) + (\beta_1 + u_{1j})\, t_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ij}. \]

\(j\) is the person, the child, or the enclosure. \(i\) is the wave. \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) are the mean intercept and the mean slope. \(u_{0j}\) and \(u_{1j}\) are the cluster’s departures, mean zero, usually Gaussian.

The sketch replaces a separate line for each of sixteen children with these four parameters. Ignoring \(j\) treats the waves as independent, and the interval uses the wrong variance. The same hierarchy is what lets a longitudinal sample be a multilevel model.

Read the model callout: random intercept \(u_{0j}\) and random slope \(u_{1j}\) on time inside cluster \(j\). Sixteen separate lines become four population parameters plus cluster departures. Ignoring \(j\) is independence across waves—the wrong standard error. This is the generative story behind the spaghetti plot two slides ahead.

The call, then the picture

Warming sits on the enclosure. Time sits on the wave. The excerpt is from generate-slide-figures.R. The second call is the nlme version of the same mean, with an AR(1) residual. It is not the fit drawn on the next slide.

lmer-call.R

lmer(
  Y ~ time * warming + (time | enclosure),
  REML = TRUE
)

nlme::lme(
  Y ~ time * warming,
  random = ~ time | enclosure,
  correlation = nlme::corAR1(form = ~ time | enclosure),
  method = "REML"
)

A farm block under a split-plot is the same (1 | cluster) term. Chapter 29 of A Guide on Data Analysis fits that term by REML, and tests the whole-plot factor against the farm variance.

Walk lmer(Y ~ time * warming + (time | enclosure), REML = TRUE) first: warming on enclosure, time on the wave. The nlme block adds corAR1(form = ~ time | enclosure)—same mean structure, explicit residual correlation. Say the second call is not the fit drawn on the next slide. Posit chapter 29 links farm blocks to (1|cluster) for split-plot thinking.

Twelve enclosures, two slopes

Illustrative, seed 20261005, not a SPRUCE fit. The lines are lmer(Y ~ time * warming + (time | enclosure), REML = TRUE). One mean structure, and a departure \(u_{0j}\) and \(u_{1j}\) for each enclosure.

Pair with the code slide: this is the saved simulation at seed 20261005, not SPRUCE data. Point at ambient versus warmed colours and per-enclosure lines—each line is \(u_{0j}\) and \(u_{1j}\) around the shared time * warming mean. Thirty seconds if you are short on time; the estimand is still enclosure-level warming over time, not independent flux points.

Choosing the runs

Choose the runs before the measurements

A design of experiments picks the combinations you will run, before any \(Y\) is recorded. The organising question is the objective, not the historical name of the matrix.

A smaller matrix buys its size by giving something up. The usual sacrifice is aliasing: two effects share one column, so the fit cannot tell them apart. The four families below are the ones the overview treats as the working set: fractional factorials, definitive screening, a response surface, and an optimal design.

NIST’s selection chapter is the map: how do you select an experimental design?

DOE chooses \(x\) combinations before any \(Y\) is measured—the objective drives the matrix, not the historical name. Aliasing is the price of a smaller design: two effects share a column. Name the four families on the slide as the working set for the next four slides, then point to NIST as the map.

A fraction spends the interactions

A full factorial of \(k\) two-level factors needs \(2^k\) runs. Ten factors need \(1024\). A fractional factorial keeps \(2^{k-p}\) runs. Five factors at a quarter fraction need \(2^{5-2} = 8\), against \(32\) for the full \(2^5\).

Resolution says which effects are aliased. A low resolution is a screen for main effects. A high resolution leaves the interactions you care about separable. NIST’s note on resolution is here.

Use the numbers on the slide: \(2^{5-2}=8\) runs versus \(32\) for a full \(2^5\). Resolution vocabulary tells you which interactions are sacrificed—low resolution screens mains; high resolution protects interactions you still need. Students sometimes treat a fraction as “the same factorial but cheaper” without reading the alias table.

Going further. A fraction is defined by generators: the half fraction of \(2^3\) in the sketch uses \(C = AB\), so the defining relation is \(I = ABC\) and every effect is aliased with its product with \(ABC\) (\(A\) with \(BC\), \(B\) with \(AC\), \(C\) with \(AB\)). The resolution is the length of the shortest word in the defining relation: resolution III aliases main effects with two-factor interactions, IV aliases main effects only with three-factor interactions but two-factor interactions with each other, and V keeps main effects and two-factor interactions clear of each other. Among designs of equal resolution, minimum aberration (Fries and Hunter, 1980, Technometrics) picks the one with the fewest short words. An aliased pair is estimated as a sum, so the fit is unbiased for that sum, not for either effect, and a fold-over can break the aliasing afterwards. Box, Hunter and Hunter, Statistics for Experimenters (2nd edition, 2005), chapters 5–6, is the classic treatment.

A definitive screen also sees a curve

Plackett–Burman is the classical screen: \(11\) two-level factors in \(12\) runs, with main effects aliased with two-factor interactions. NIST describes it as a design for when the main effects are the focus.

A definitive screening design is the modern alternative for continuous factors. The run count is about \(2k+1\), so \(14\) factors need about \(29\) runs rather than \(2^{14}\). Each factor has levels \(-1\), \(0\), and \(+1\), so a quadratic term \(\beta_{11} x^2\) can be seen. JMP’s account: main effects are orthogonal to two-factor interactions, and those interactions are not completely aliased with each other. Definitive screening designs.

Contrast Plackett–Burman’s \(11\) factors in \(12\) runs with main effects aliased to two-factor interactions against definitive screening’s three levels per factor. The \(0\) level is what lets a quadratic \(\beta_{11}x^2\) appear—Plackett–Burman cannot do that. Quote \(2k+1\) when someone asks how many runs for fourteen factors.

Going further. Jones and Nachtsheim (2011, Journal of Quality Technology, “A class of three-level designs for definitive screening in the presence of second-order effects”) built the design from a conference matrix \(\mathbf{C}\): the runs are \(\mathbf{C}\), \(-\mathbf{C}\) and a centre run, which is why there are \(2k + 1\). The fold-over makes every main effect orthogonal to every two-factor interaction and to every quadratic term, so main-effect estimates are unbiased by any second-order effect. Quadratic terms are estimable, but with low power, and they are correlated with each other; a two-factor interaction is partially aliased with others rather than completely. Plackett–Burman designs (Plackett and Burman, 1946, Biometrika) have “complex aliasing” instead: each two-factor interaction is spread over several main-effect columns with coefficients like \(\pm 1/3\), which is harder to unpick than the clean aliasing of a regular fraction. Both rely on effect sparsity: only a few factors are active.

A surface needs three levels

Once a few factors remain, the question moves from “which factor?” to “where is the optimum?”. The working model is quadratic: a linear term, a square, and a product for each pair.

  • A central composite design is a factorial, plus axial points \((\pm\alpha, 0)\) and \((0, \pm\alpha)\), plus centre points.

  • A Box–Behnken design also estimates that quadratic surface, and it avoids the corner where every factor is at its extreme.

Both are in JMP’s introduction to DOE.

After screening, the question is “where is the optimum?”—hence linear, square, and product terms. Fragment one: central composite adds axial and centre points. Fragment two: Box–Behnken avoids the all-extremes corner. Both need more than two levels per factor; link back to SPRUCE’s continuous warming grid as a field analogue of “shape”, not necessarily a CCD.

Going further. The second-order model is \(\mu = \beta_0 + \sum_k \beta_k x_k + \sum_k \beta_{kk} x_k^2 + \sum_{k<l} \beta_{kl} x_k x_l\), and the stationary point is \(\mathbf{x}_s = -\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{B}^{-1}\mathbf{b}\), whose nature (maximum, minimum or saddle) is read from the eigenvalues of \(\mathbf{B}\) in canonical analysis. A central composite design is rotatable, so the prediction variance depends only on the distance from the centre, when \(\alpha = (n_F)^{1/4}\) with \(n_F\) the number of factorial points; \(\alpha = 1\) gives the face-centred version that stays inside the cube. Replicated centre points give a pure-error estimate and a test of curvature. The method goes back to Box and Wilson (1951, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, “On the experimental attainment of optimum conditions”); Myers, Montgomery and Anderson-Cook, Response Surface Methodology (4th edition, 2016), is the current text.

An optimal design is computed for the constraint

D-optimal, I-optimal, and A-optimal designs are algorithm-built matrices. They are the modern choice when the run budget is tight, the factors are a mix of continuous and categorical, or the experimental region is an awkward shape.

The matrix is less readable than a textbook factorial. The criterion is explicit: D-optimality, for example, targets the precision of the coefficient estimates. A mixture, where the factors are parts of a constant sum, needs its own geometry rather than one of these factorials.

When the region is awkward or the budget is tight, the computer builds the matrix against D-, I-, or A-optimality. Say explicitly that the criterion replaces the pretty symmetry of a textbook factorial. Mixture designs are the exception named on the slide—proportions summing to one are not a standard factorial cube.

Going further. For a linear model with design matrix \(\mathbf{X}\), \(\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}) = \sigma^2(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\). D-optimality maximises \(\det(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X})\), which minimises the volume of the joint confidence ellipsoid; A-optimality minimises \(\mathrm{tr}\big((\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\big)\), the average coefficient variance; I-optimality minimises the prediction variance averaged over the region, the natural choice when the aim is a response surface. The Kiefer–Wolfowitz equivalence theorem (1960, Canadian Journal of Mathematics) states that, for approximate designs, D-optimality and G-optimality (minimising the maximum prediction variance) coincide, and the maximum standardised prediction variance then equals the number of parameters \(p\), which gives a certificate of optimality. The criterion is optimal only for the model you specify: a D-optimal design for a straight line has no interior points and cannot detect curvature. For a GLM, \(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{X}\) depends on the unknown \(\boldsymbol\beta\), so designs are locally optimal or Bayesian. Atkinson, Donev and Tobias, Optimum Experimental Designs, with SAS (2007), is the reference.

A decision tree for the matrix

  • Objective, chosen before any measurement
    • Screen, when many factors might matter: a fractional factorial, Plackett–Burman, or a definitive screening design
      • Interactions, once a few factors remain: a full or high-resolution factorial
        • Optimise: a central composite, a Box–Behnken, or an optimal design
    • Taguchi, when the target is robustness to uncontrolled noise
    • Mixture, when the factors are parts of a constant sum

Walk the nested bullets top-down: objective before measurement, then screen versus optimise branches. Taguchi and mixture are leaves students may never use but should recognise on a methods form. This tree is the thirty-second recap before Schielzeth’s figures make crossing and nesting visual.

Eight minutes: name the plan 📝

For your study, or for SPRUCE, write which row of the map it is, and what the plan spent.

  • screen, factorial, gradient, or mixed model of units
  • what was given up: aliasing, a missing cross, or too few units for the parameters

Eight minutes. SPRUCE is the worked answer because the warming grid is a designed shape, not a screen of dozens of factors.

One reading: the SPRUCE grid

SPRUCE is not a fractional factorial. Two factors were built, and the combinations exist.

  • Warming is a gradient: five levels, used as a regression
  • CO\(_2\) is crossed with warming on the same enclosure
  • Ten enclosures. A slope, a CO\(_2\) shift, and their product are a few parameters. A separate mean for every cell is not
  • Nothing is aliased. The limit is \(n\), not resolution

CA-SYS is the other shape: systems sit in zones, and two zones contain only one practice. That is a missing cross, which is a design fact, not a fractional factorial you chose.

Count parameters on the board: intercept, warming slope, CO2, interaction, against ten enclosures. Then say the CA-SYS missing cross in one sentence. Do not open JMP.

Causal estimands

⚖️ Twenty minutes. Simpson, the DAG roles, and the network search. A Bayesian reading of the same mean is in the close.

A coefficient is not an intervention

SPRUCE assigns warming and \(\mathrm{CO}_2\). A slope on assigned warming estimates the effect of that assignment, in that bog, under the design assumptions.

An observational regression of taxon counts on organic carbon does not estimate “the effect of setting carbon to a new value”, unless the adjustment set matches the causal question.

Randomisation is a design fact. Adding covariates is not a substitute for it.

SPRUCE warming and \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) are assigned; the slope answers that assignment in that bog. CA-SYS organic-carbon regression is observational—no \(do(\text{carbon})\) without the right adjustment set. Covariates adjust associations; they do not recreate randomisation. This slide opens the causal hour. Simpson is next.

Going further. In the potential-outcomes notation, each unit has a response \(Y(x)\) for every level \(x\) it could receive, and the average causal effect is \(\mathbb{E}\{Y(x_1)\} - \mathbb{E}\{Y(x_0)\}\). The regression contrast \(\mathbb{E}(Y \mid x_1) - \mathbb{E}(Y \mid x_0)\) equals it under three identification conditions: consistency (\(Y = Y(x)\) for the level actually received), conditional exchangeability (\(Y(x) \perp X \mid \mathbf{L}\) for an adjustment set \(\mathbf{L}\)), and positivity (\(\Pr(X = x \mid \mathbf{L}) > 0\) for every stratum). Randomisation makes exchangeability hold by design with \(\mathbf{L}\) empty; in observational data it is an untestable assumption about \(\mathbf{L}\). The standard references are Hernán and Robins, Causal Inference: What If, and Imbens and Rubin, Causal Inference for Statistics, Social, and Biomedical Sciences.

Simpson

Two hospitals, one survival rate

François Giltaire, Le paradoxe de Simpson. A public-health report prints one number per hospital. Survival is 86% at A and 79% at B. The booking that follows from those two numbers is A.

State the two overall rates—86% at A, 79% at B—and let the room say “choose A”. Do not spoil the strata yet; the next slide breaks the table. Giltaire is the narrative source on the slide.

Inside each severity, B is higher

A takes mostly light cases. B takes mostly severe cases. Each hospital has 1000 patients.

Light cases Severe cases Overall
A 90% of 800 70% of 200 86%
B 95% of 200 75% of 800 79%

Light cases: B is above A. Severe cases: B is above A. The single published rate still ranks A above B.

Walk the table: A has 800 light and 200 severe; B has 200 light and 800 severe—1000 patients each. Within light, B beats A; within severe, B beats A again. Ask why the headline still favours A; the weight slide answers with arithmetic.

The overall rate is a weighted mean

The overall rate is the subgroup rates weighted by how many patients sit in each subgroup.

\[ \frac{800 \times 0.9 + 200 \times 0.7}{800 + 200} = 86\% \]

\[ \frac{200 \times 0.95 + 800 \times 0.75}{200 + 800} = 79\% \]

The denominators match. A puts a weight of \(n = 800\) on the light cases, where the rates are high. B puts a weight of \(n = 200\) on those same cases. That difference in weights is enough to reverse the overall ranking.

Read the two displayed fractions that yield 86% and 79%. Point at the \(800\) versus \(200\) weights on light cases—the subgroup rates favour B, but the mix favours A overall. This is the mechanism CA-SYS will reuse without necessarily reversing the sign.

Going further. The remedy is standardisation: apply each hospital’s stratum rates to one common case mix. With the pooled mix of 1000 light and 1000 severe cases, A gives \(0.5 \times 0.90 + 0.5 \times 0.70 = 80\%\) and B gives \(0.5 \times 0.95 + 0.5 \times 0.75 = 85\%\), so B is ahead once the weights are equal. In causal terms this is the back-door adjustment formula, \(\Pr\{Y = 1 \mid do(x)\} = \sum_s \Pr(Y = 1 \mid x, s)\,\Pr(s)\), valid when severity \(S\) closes every back-door path from hospital to survival. Whether to pool or to stratify is not a statistical question: Pearl showed that the same table can call for either answer depending on whether the third variable is a confounder or a mediator (Pearl, “Comment: Understanding Simpson’s Paradox”, The American Statistician, 2014). Direct standardisation in epidemiology is the same computation, with a reference population chosen in advance.

Severity mixes two hospitals that are not the same

Severity changes which hospital the patients go to, and it changes the survival rate. Pooling the light cases with the severe cases compares hospitals that did not treat the same mix.

The paradox, in one sentence: a trend that holds in every subgroup can reverse once the subgroups are pooled, because the subgroups do not have the same proportions. The soil version is the same arithmetic on CA-SYS.

DAG: severity \(\to\) hospital and severity \(\to\) survival; hospital \(\to\) survival. Pooling mixes severities with different hospital proportions—that opens a non-causal association. Read the one-sentence paradox, then jump to [#sec-casys-confounding] for tillage zones where weights shift the contrast without a full reversal.

The same arithmetic, on the soil table

Contrast Samples No-till minus tilled 95% interval
All zones pooled 595 \(+47.5\) OTUs \(-7.5\) to \(+102.6\)
Mixed zone only 226 \(+80.3\) OTUs \(-6.0\) to \(+166.7\)

Work through the two rows. The pooled contrast uses 595 samples and gives +47.5 OTUs. Restricting to the mixed zone, where no-till and tilled fields sit side by side, nearly doubles it to +80.3 on 226 samples. The hospital table had a reversal; this is the same mechanism without one, which is the more common case in practice: the weights differ, so the pooled number is not the contrast you wanted. Say clearly that both intervals include zero, so neither row is a detected difference. The honest sentence is that the practice contrast is imprecise here and that its point estimate depends on which samples you compare.

Why the two rows differ

The CA-SYS zones are not a nuisance; they are part of the platform’s design.

Zone No-till samples Tilled samples
Mixed 114 112
No-till zone 171 0
Tilled zone 0 198

Two of the three zones contain only one practice. In those rows the tillage contrast is not identified at all: any difference between them is also a difference between places.

This is a positivity, or overlap, failure, and it is worth naming. Within the no-till zone there is no tilled sample to compare against, so no amount of modelling recovers a within-zone contrast there. A regression with zone as a covariate will still print a tillage coefficient; it will be driven entirely by the 226 mixed-zone samples plus an extrapolation. The mixed zone exists because the designers wanted to test the spatial arrangement of practices, which makes it the right place to read the contrast.

Going further. Positivity requires \(0 < \Pr(X = x \mid \mathbf{L} = \mathbf{l}) < 1\) for every stratum \(\mathbf{l}\) of the adjustment set that the target population contains. Here \(\Pr(\text{tilled} \mid \text{no-till zone}) = 0\) is a structural violation, fixed by the design, not a random zero that a larger sample would fill. Two honest responses exist: change the estimand to the population where overlap holds (the mixed zone), or keep the full population and accept that the answer rests on a parametric extrapolation. Weighting estimators make the problem visible, since the inverse probability weight \(1/\Pr(X = x \mid \mathbf{L})\) is infinite there. Petersen and colleagues, “Diagnosing and responding to violations in the positivity assumption” (Statistical Methods in Medical Research, 2012), is the standard treatment.

The arrow pattern behind both tables

Zone decides which practice a field receives, and the soil in a zone also acts on the community. That is the hospital graph with new labels: severity mixes two hospitals.

Point out that this diagram is an assumption, not a result. It says zone acts on richness through something other than tillage, which is plausible because soil type is unbalanced across zones, but the data cannot prove the arrow. That is the message of the DAG slides that follow.

Going further. In this graph the path practice \(\leftarrow\) zone \(\to\) richness is a back-door path: it starts with an arrow into the treatment. Pearl’s back-door criterion says a set \(\mathbf{L}\) identifies the effect of practice on \(Y\) when no member of \(\mathbf{L}\) is a descendant of practice and \(\mathbf{L}\) blocks every back-door path; here \(\mathbf{L} = \{\text{zone}\}\) qualifies. The identifying formula is then \(\mathbb{E}\{Y \mid do(x)\} = \sum_{z} \mathbb{E}(Y \mid x, z)\,\Pr(z)\), and the previous slide shows that two of the three terms \(\mathbb{E}(Y \mid x, z)\) are not estimable. A valid adjustment set therefore needs both a correct graph and positivity within it. The reference is Pearl, Causality (2nd edition, 2009), chapter 3.

Roles on a graph

The DAG is a set of assumptions

Johannes Hertel, Linking statistics, computational biology and biochemistry, lists three assumptions before the arrows can be read as causes.

Assumption

There is a DAG that is a causal representation of the system. A variable is independent of its non-effects given its direct causes. The only conditional independences in the data are the ones that DAG states.

The second sentence is his causal Markov condition. The third is faithfulness. He notes that a complete measurement of every variable in the graph is generally impossible, so the practical question is which variables the analysis has to include.

Read the assumption callout slowly: causal DAG, Markov (independence given parents), faithfulness (only those independences). Incomplete measurement is the practical punchline—which nodes must enter the model? The six numbered role slides after the fork and the chain answer that question one third variable at a time.

Going further. The causal Markov condition states that each variable is independent of its non-descendants given its parents, which is equivalent to the factorisation \(p(v_1, \ldots, v_K) = \prod_k p(v_k \mid \mathrm{pa}_k)\) and to “d-separation implies independence”. Faithfulness is the converse: every conditional independence in the distribution is a d-separation in the graph. It fails when two paths cancel exactly, for example a direct effect \(+\beta\) and an indirect effect \(-\beta\); the set of such parameter values has Lebesgue measure zero, which is the usual justification, but near-cancellation makes tests unreliable in finite samples (Uhler and colleagues, Annals of Statistics, 2013). A third, often implicit, condition is causal sufficiency: no unmeasured common cause of two measured variables. Spirtes, Glymour and Scheines, Causation, Prediction, and Search (2000), is the standard statement of all three.

Set up the puzzle: one conditional-independence pattern, two directed stories. Read the shared statement about \(T\), \(X\), and \(Z\) without showing arrows yet. Ask the room what differs between fork and chain if \(Z\perp X\mid T\) in both—the next two slides answer with arrow direction.

Going further. The graphical rule behind this is d-separation. A path between two nodes is blocked by a conditioning set \(S\) when it contains a chain \(A \to B \to C\) or a fork \(A \leftarrow B \to C\) with \(B \in S\), or a collider \(A \to B \leftarrow C\) with neither \(B\) nor any descendant of \(B\) in \(S\). Two nodes are d-separated given \(S\) when every path between them is blocked; under the causal Markov condition, d-separation implies conditional independence in every distribution the graph generates. Fork and chain produce the same d-separation statements, so no test on observational data can tell them apart; only a collider leaves a distinct signature. The reference is Pearl, Probabilistic Reasoning in Intelligent Systems (1988), and Koller and Friedman, Probabilistic Graphical Models (2009), chapter 3.

Role 1 · A confounder causes both \(X\) and \(Y\)

Carbon and the taxon both respond to moisture, so the unadjusted slope of \(Y\) on \(X\) mixes the blue path with the orange back-door path.

Adjust for it, by design or in the model. Otherwise the coefficient is not the effect of \(X\). Simpson’s hospitals and the CA-SYS zones are this graph.

Point at the orange back-door path \(X \leftarrow Z \to Y\) first, then at the blue arrow. Age between a disease phenotype and a metabolite is Hertel’s example; soil moisture between carbon and a taxon is ours. Ask the room what happens if moisture were instead the way carbon acts on the taxon: then it is role 4, and adjusting removes part of the effect.

Going further. Pearl’s back-door criterion: a set \(\mathbf{L}\) identifies the effect of \(X\) on \(Y\) when no member of \(\mathbf{L}\) is a descendant of \(X\) and \(\mathbf{L}\) blocks every path that starts with an arrow into \(X\). The identifying formula is \(\mathbb{E}\{Y \mid do(x)\} = \sum_{z} \mathbb{E}(Y \mid x, z)\Pr(z)\), the standardisation that reversed the hospital ranking. Under the null of no effect the fork gives \(X \perp Y \mid Z\), which is why conditioning on \(Z\) removes the spurious association. An unmeasured confounder cannot be adjusted for; the sensitivity slide at the end of this block bounds how strong it would have to be (Pearl, Causality, 2nd edition, 2009, chapter 3).

Role 2 · A collider is caused by both

Conditioning on \(Z\), or keeping only the samples that passed it, opens the orange path and creates an \(X\)–\(Y\) association. Restricting a study to healthy people is the selection-bias version.

Leave it out. Conditioning on a collider anyway is called overmatching.

Collider: \(X\to Z\leftarrow Y\), a v-structure in the Bayesian-network notes. Hertel’s example is inflammation. Here the filter on sequencing depth is the collider: if both carbon and the taxon raise the read count, the samples that survive the filter carry an association the field never had.

The graph without the blue arrow factorises as \(p(x,y,z)=p(x)\,p(y)\,p(z\mid x,y)\), so \(p(x,y)=p(x)p(y)\) and \(X\perp Y\). After selecting on \(Z\), \(p(x,y\mid z)=p(z\mid x,y)\,p(x)\,p(y)/p(z)\), which does not factor into a function of \(x\) times a function of \(y\), so \(X\not\perp Y\mid Z\).

Going further. The classical case is Berkson’s bias (Berkson, Biometrics Bulletin, 1946): two diseases independent in the population become negatively associated among hospital patients, because admission is a common effect of both. Adjusting for a descendant of a collider opens the path too, more weakly. Unlike confounding bias, collider bias cannot be removed by collecting more covariates after the selection; it has to be prevented at the design stage, or corrected with inverse probability of selection weights when the selection model is known. Hernán, Hernández-Díaz and Robins, “A structural approach to selection bias” (Epidemiology, 2004), is the reference.

Role 3 · A variance factor touches only \(Y\)

A batch effect adds noise to \(Y\) without creating an \(X\)–\(Y\) correlation. It can hide one.

Adjust for it, for power: by blocking in the design, or as a term in the model. The coefficient of \(X\) is unbiased either way; only its interval changes.

DAG: \(X\to Y\) and \(Z\to Y\) only—no \(Z\to X\). Adjust for precision, not because \(Z\) confounds. This is the blocking argument of the design hour in graph form.

The graph factorises as \(p(x,y,z)=p(x)\,p(z)\,p(y\mid x,z)\). There is no back-door path, so the \(X\) slope is identified with or without \(Z\). The law of total variance splits the noise: \(\mathrm{Var}(Y\mid X)=\mathbb{E}\{\mathrm{Var}(Y\mid X,Z)\mid X\}+\mathrm{Var}\{\mathbb{E}(Y\mid X,Z)\mid X\}\). A batch effect sits in the second term, and conditioning on \(Z\) drops it. On a non-identity link the story is subtler: for a logistic model, omitting a precision variable attenuates the conditional odds ratio, because odds ratios are not collapsible, even though \(Z \perp X\).

Role 4 · A mediator carries part of the effect

The orange path is indirect. The blue arrow is direct. The total effect of assigned warming is both together.

Leave it out for the total effect. Adjusting for productivity estimates something else, and only under further assumptions. Write the path you mean before you add the covariate.

Warming \(\to\) productivity \(\to\) flux is indirect; warming \(\to\) flux is direct. The total effect of assigned warming does not condition on productivity. Adjusting for productivity targets a different estimand—say “write the path first” before opening lm().

Going further. With nested potential outcomes \(Y(x, M(x'))\), the total effect splits exactly into a natural direct effect, \(\mathbb{E}\{Y(1, M(0))\} - \mathbb{E}\{Y(0, M(0))\}\), and a natural indirect effect, \(\mathbb{E}\{Y(1, M(1))\} - \mathbb{E}\{Y(1, M(0))\}\). Randomising warming identifies the total effect, but not these two pieces: they also need no unmeasured confounding of the mediator–outcome relation, and no such confounder affected by warming itself (the cross-world assumption). If a soil variable drives both productivity and flux, conditioning on productivity opens a collider path and biases even the direct effect. The usual references are Robins and Greenland (1992), Pearl, “Direct and indirect effects” (2001), and VanderWeele, Explanation in Causal Inference (2015).

Role 5 · A moderator changes the effect

The orange arrow points at the blue arrow, not at a node: \(Z\) changes how much \(Y\) moves when \(X\) moves.

Model an interaction, or report each stratum. Matching on \(Z\) does not do that job, and the sample must be large enough for the interaction.

Hertel’s example is sex: women and men may show different metabolite profiles in response to a disease. Ours: the warming effect on flux may depend on how far down the water table sits. There is no new conditional independence to block or open—a moderator is neither a fork nor a collider.

Write \(\mathbb{E}(Y\mid X=x,Z=z)=\beta_0+\beta_1 x+\beta_2 z+\beta_3 xz\). Then \(\beta_3\) is the change in the \(X\) slope per unit of \(Z\). Matching on \(Z\) mixes the stratum slopes; it does not estimate \(\beta_3\).

Going further. Effect modification is scale-dependent: on a log link, \(\beta_3 = 0\) means the rate ratio is the same in each stratum of \(Z\), yet the difference in \(\mu\) can still differ between strata, and the reverse holds on the identity scale. So “no interaction” must always name the link \(g\). VanderWeele distinguishes effect modification (\(Z\) merely observed) from causal interaction (joint intervention on \(X\) and \(Z\)), which needs \(Z\) itself to be unconfounded. With a balanced binary \(Z\), the standard error of \(\beta_3\) is roughly twice that of a main effect, so detecting an interaction of the same size takes about four times the sample (Gelman, Hill and Vehtari, Regression and Other Stories, 2020).

Role 6 · An instrument touches only \(X\)

\(Z\) moves \(X\) and reaches \(Y\) only through \(X\). It creates no spurious \(X\)–\(Y\) correlation.

Optional. It does not need to enter the regression. Some designs are built around it, when \(X\) and \(Y\) share a confounder nobody measured.

Instrument path: \(Z\to X\to Y\) with no arrow from \(Z\) to \(Y\). Students confuse instruments with confounders because both touch \(X\); check for a \(Z\to Y\) edge.

The graph factorises as \(p(z,x,y)=p(z)\,p(x\mid z)\,p(y\mid x)\), so \(p(y\mid x,z)=p(y\mid x)\), which is \(Z\perp Y\mid X\). A confounder would add \(Z\to Y\) and break that equality.

Going further. The three instrument conditions are relevance (\(Z \not\perp X\)), exclusion (\(Z\) acts on \(Y\) only through \(X\)) and independence (\(Z \perp U\) for the unmeasured confounder \(U\)); only the first is testable. With a binary \(Z\) and a homogeneous linear effect, the Wald estimator \(\{\mathbb{E}(Y \mid Z=1) - \mathbb{E}(Y \mid Z=0)\}/\{\mathbb{E}(X \mid Z=1) - \mathbb{E}(X \mid Z=0)\}\) recovers the effect of \(X\); two-stage least squares is its multivariable form. With heterogeneous effects it identifies only the local average effect among units whose \(X\) responds to \(Z\), under monotonicity (Imbens and Angrist, Econometrica, 1994). Mendelian randomisation is the genetic-variant case on this slide.

Adjust what the role requires

The control list, for an explanatory analysis.

  • Role 1, a confounder: control it, by matching or in the model, or the interpretation is wrong.

  • Role 2, a collider: leave it out.

  • Role 3, a variance factor: control it, for power.

  • Role 4, a mediator: leave it out, unless the question is that path.

  • Role 5, a moderator: an interaction or a stratum, not a match alone.

  • Role 6, an instrument: optional. Some designs are built around it.

Step the six fragments as a control checklist: confounder in, collider out, variance factor in for power, mediator out unless that path is the estimand, moderator needs interaction, instrument optional. About one minute if you step each line—pause after collider versus confounder because that pair is what exams test.

Sensitivity is the causal report

For an observational claim, say what would have to be true for the conclusion to change:

  • a missing confounder associated with both \(x\) and \(Y\) at a stated strength
  • a different adjustment set from the same diagram
  • a different family, if the mean is sensitive to the variance assumption
  • a different prior, if the fit is Bayesian and the sample is small

SPRUCE still needs a sensitivity story for the chamber itself: the design page monitors chamberless areas because the enclosure is not identical to an open bog. The pitfalls card is show that the conclusion can move.

Observational claims need explicit what-ifs: unmeasured confounder strength, alternate adjustment sets, family change, prior change for small Bayesian fits. SPRUCE chamberless plots are the designed sensitivity for enclosure versus open bog—cite the design page line on the slide. Link [#sec-sensitivity] in pitfalls for the reporting habit.

Going further. The first bullet has a closed-form answer. For an observed risk ratio \(RR\) (or a rate ratio from a log-link GLM), the E-value \(RR + \sqrt{RR(RR - 1)}\) is the minimum strength of association, on the risk-ratio scale, that an unmeasured confounder would need with both treatment and outcome to move the estimate to the null, conditional on the measured covariates (VanderWeele and Ding, Annals of Internal Medicine, 2017). It rests on the Ding–VanderWeele bounding factor, which makes no assumption about the confounder’s distribution, so it is conservative. Rosenbaum’s sensitivity parameter \(\Gamma\) plays the same role for matched designs: it bounds how far the odds of treatment can differ between two matched units because of an unobserved covariate (Rosenbaum, Observational Studies, 2002). For the Bayesian bullet, the analogue is to report the posterior under at least two priors and say whether the decision changes.

Causally orient the edges

A direct link is not a direction

The Bayesian-network course notes separate two graphs. A dependency network joins two variables that still share a statistical relationship once the others are accounted for. That removes indirect co-variation. It does not say which way the link runs.

A regulatory direction needs a further claim, in the notes’ words: a change in \(X\) produces a change in \(Y\), and a change in \(Y\) does not change \(X\). That is the same gap as Hertel’s fork and chain, one independence, two causal stories.

Dependency networks remove indirect association once other variables are accounted for—they do not orient edges. Regulatory direction needs asymmetry under intervention, as the notes quote. Tie back to [#sec-same-ci]: statistics alone did not pick fork versus chain.

Going further. For Gaussian data the dependency network is the Gaussian graphical model: an edge \(A - B\) is absent exactly when the partial correlation of \(A\) and \(B\) given all other variables is zero, which is a zero in the precision matrix \(\Sigma^{-1}\). The graphical lasso (Friedman, Hastie and Tibshirani, Biostatistics, 2008) estimates a sparse \(\Sigma^{-1}\) when the number of variables exceeds the sample size. This undirected graph is the moral graph of any DAG that generated the data: it contains every DAG edge plus an edge between co-parents of a collider, so it can show a link that no causal arrow supports. For compositional counts such as 16S data, partial correlations on raw proportions are biased by the sum constraint, which is why methods such as SPIEC-EASI work on log-ratios first (Kurtz and colleagues, PLoS Computational Biology, 2015). Lauritzen, Graphical Models (1996), is the reference text.

Three graphs, one distribution

With \(Z\) between \(X\) and \(Y\), and no direct arrow from \(X\) to \(Y\), the notes count four directed acyclic graphs. Three of them encode the same conditional independences. Those three are one Markov equivalence class, drawn as a completed partially directed acyclic graph: an edge is directed only when the direction is identified, and left undirected when it is not.

Statistics on the observational distribution will not separate the three. The notes’ next step is a causal analysis.

With \(Z\) between \(X\) and \(Y\) and no \(X\to Y\), four DAGs collapse to one Markov equivalence class of three—CPDAG leaves some edges undirected. Observational data cannot pick among the three; the notes point to causal analysis next. Knock-out and time series are the two escapes on the following slides.

Going further. Verma and Pearl (1990) proved that two DAGs are Markov equivalent exactly when they have the same skeleton and the same v-structures, that is the same unshielded colliders \(A \to B \leftarrow C\) with \(A\) and \(C\) non-adjacent. Here the three graphs without a collider at \(Z\) share skeleton \(X - Z - Y\) and have no v-structure, while \(X \to Z \leftarrow Y\) has one, so it sits alone in its class. The CPDAG (or essential graph) directs an edge when every member of the class agrees on it; Meek’s rules (1995) propagate those compelled orientations from the v-structures without creating a new collider or a cycle. With linear structural equations and non-Gaussian errors the class can shrink to one graph (LiNGAM, Shimizu and colleagues, 2006), which is one way extra assumptions buy direction.

A knock-out supplies the direction

When the graph was not drawn by an expert, the notes’ first source of direction is a perturbation. If knocking out \(X\) changes \(Y\), the notes write \(X \to Y\). They read that experiment as an intervention on \(X\).

It is empirical, and it does not need a fitted network. It is a wet-lab result. Orienting a whole network this way needs many perturbations, which the notes say does not scale.

Perturbation first: knock out \(X\), watch \(Y\), write \(X\to Y\) and link to \(do(X)\). Wet-lab empirical direction without fitting a network—but scaling to whole networks needs many knockouts, which the notes dismiss. Contrast with passive observational equivalence on the previous slide.

Going further. A perfect intervention on \(X\) cuts every arrow into \(X\), so comparing the distribution of \(Y\) with and without the knock-out tests \(X \to Y\) against \(Y \to X\) directly; it also distinguishes members of the same Markov equivalence class. Eberhardt, Glymour and Scheines (2005) showed that \(p - 1\) single-variable interventions are sufficient, and in the worst case necessary, to orient every edge of a \(p\)-node graph, which is the “does not scale” remark in formal terms. Knock-outs are rarely perfect: compensation, off-target effects and incomplete silencing make them soft interventions, which change \(p(x \mid \mathrm{pa}_X)\) rather than fix \(X\). Mixing observational and interventional data under a known intervention target is what the GIES algorithm of Hauser and Bühlmann (JMLR, 2012) does.

Time supplies the direction

The other source in the notes is a series. The regression is the dependency-network regression, moved forward one time step.

Model

\[ Y(t+1) \approx a_1 X_1(t) + \cdots + a_k X_k(t). \]

If \(a_i \ne 0\), then \(X_i\) regulates \(Y\) from one time to the next. The notes call this a dynamic Bayesian network: an initial state, the same transition from time to time, and the chain unrolled.

Read the model callout: \(Y(t+1)\) regressed on \(X_1(t),\ldots,X_k(t)\). Non-zero \(a_i\) means \(X_i\) regulates \(Y\) forward in time—direction from lag, not from partial correlation alone. Dynamic BN unrolls the same transition; link to flux time series only if you stay within the slide’s regression wording.

Going further. Testing \(a_i = 0\) in this lagged regression is Granger causality (Granger, Econometrica, 1969): \(X_i\) Granger-causes \(Y\) when its past improves the prediction of \(Y\) beyond the past of every other included series. It is a statement about prediction, and it equals a causal claim only when all common drivers are in the regression, the sampling interval is shorter than the causal lag, and there is no instantaneous effect within a time step; a slow, unmeasured seasonal driver produces spurious lags. A dynamic Bayesian network adds the assumptions that the transition is first-order Markov and stationary, so one two-slice graph describes the whole series (Murphy, Dynamic Bayesian Networks, PhD thesis, 2002). Because arrows only point forward in time, the acyclicity restriction is lifted across slices, which is how feedback loops re-enter.

Three complementary approaches to learn the structure of a DAG

  • Constraint-based: test a conditional independence. If the test rejects independence, the nodes are joined.

  • Score-based: give each candidate graph a score for how well it describes the data, and maximise the score.

  • Hybrid: learn the skeleton from the constraints, then refine it with a score.

Marco Scutari’s benchmark, as the notes report it, for the developer of bnlearn: at small samples the constraint-based algorithms were more accurate than the score-based ones, and as accurate as the hybrids. Tabu search, a score-based method, was faster than the constraint-based algorithms and faster than simulated annealing.

Step the three items: constraint-based joins nodes when independence tests fail; score-based maximises a graph score; hybrid skeleton then score. The figure on the next slide is the same three families, with the algorithm names under each panel. These learn association structure under DAG assumptions, not causation by default.

Going further. The reference constraint-based method is the PC algorithm (Spirtes and Glymour, 1991): start from the complete undirected graph, delete an edge \(A - B\) as soon as some subset \(S\) of the current neighbours makes \(A \perp B \mid S\) pass the test, then orient the v-structures and apply Meek’s rules. Its output is a CPDAG, and it is consistent as \(n \to \infty\) under causal Markov, faithfulness, causal sufficiency and correct tests; Kalisch and Bühlmann (JMLR, 2007) extended this to sparse high-dimensional Gaussian graphs. Score-based methods maximise a decomposable score such as BIC or BDe, and the greedy equivalence search of Chickering (2002) is consistent under the same assumptions. Searching all DAGs exactly is NP-hard, which is why hill-climbing and tabu are heuristics. FCI relaxes causal sufficiency and returns a partial ancestral graph that admits latent confounders.

The three searches, named

A generated sketch. The names are the ones bnlearn groups under each search.

Walk the three panels. Constraint-based removes the edge when the conditional-independence test does not reject: PC, Grow-Shrink, IAMB, MMPC. Score-based prefers the higher-scoring DAG: hill-climbing and tabu, drawn here as the extra arrow \(B \to C\). Hybrid takes that skeleton and then scores: MMHC and RSMAX2. The picture is a generated sketch, not a fitted graph.

A searched graph is still a DAG

The notes’ limits on that search. The graph has no cycles, so a feedback loop or a self-regulation is outside it. Adding observations can change the direction of an edge. A network of thousands of nodes is too large to enumerate, and the search then needs a heuristic.

The two implementations they name are bnlearn in R and PyAgrum in Python.

Close the limits first: no cycles, so feedback is out; more data can flip an edge; thousands of nodes need a heuristic. The next slide says why the loop is excluded, then the two implementations. Causal claims still need design, \(do\), or a perturbation. Thirty seconds.

Going further. The number of DAGs on \(p\) labelled nodes grows super-exponentially (Robinson’s recursion gives about \(4.2 \times 10^{18}\) for \(p = 10\)), so exhaustive search stops at a few dozen nodes even with dynamic programming. Edge flips with more data are expected rather than alarming: the score difference between equivalent orientations is zero, and between near-equivalent ones it is small, so the bootstrap edge-frequency of Friedman, Goldszmidt and Wyner (1999), available as boot.strength() in bnlearn, is the honest report of how stable each arrow is. Cycles can be handled by unrolling in time, as on the dynamic slide, or with cyclic structural causal models, whose equilibrium semantics is more delicate (Bongers and colleagues, Annals of Statistics, 2021).

Why the graph cannot loop

A Bayesian network is a product of one conditional per node, each given its parents:

Model

\[ p(v_1, \ldots, v_K) = \prod_{k=1}^{K} p(v_k \mid \mathrm{pa}_k). \]

The product is a probability only because the nodes have a topological order: every parent comes before its child. Integrate out the last node, then the one before, and each factor sums to one. A loop \(X \to Y \to X\) has no first node, so \(p(x \mid y)\,p(y \mid x)\) need not be a joint at all. d-separation reads independences off that ordered product, so it needs the order too. Feedback comes back by unrolling in time.

One idea: the arrows must admit an order, because the factorisation is built along it. Say “integrate from the leaves upwards” and the room sees why every factor normalises. Then the loop: there is no node to start from. d-separation and the Markov condition are statements about that factorisation, so a cyclic graph has neither.

Going further. A concrete failure: take \(p(x \mid y) = \mathcal{N}(y, 1)\) and \(p(y \mid x) = \mathcal{N}(x, 1)\). Their product is proportional to \(\exp\{-(x - y)^2\}\), whose integral over the plane is infinite, so no joint density has these two conditionals. In general two conditionals are compatible only if their ratio factorises as \(a(x)/b(y)\) (Arnold and Press, Journal of the American Statistical Association, 1989), which a loop does not guarantee. The topological order also makes ancestral sampling possible: draw each node after its parents. Undirected graphs (Markov random fields) allow cycles but pay with a global normalising constant, and cyclic structural causal models are defined through equilibrium solutions rather than a factorisation (Bongers and colleagues, Annals of Statistics, 2021). The dynamic Bayesian network keeps the order by indexing the loop in time: \(X_t \to Y_{t+1} \to X_{t+2}\) is acyclic.

Two implementations

bnlearn pyAgrum
Language R Python, on the C++ library aGrUM
Structure search The long catalogue: PC, Grow-Shrink, IAMB, MMPC, hill-climbing, tabu, MMHC, RSMAX2 Hill-climbing, tabu, MIIC and 3off2; PC and FCI in recent releases
Inference Conditional queries. Exact for discrete and Gaussian networks; approximate otherwise Lazy propagation and other junction-tree methods, plus sampling. Exact inference is the main engine
Also Bootstrap of the graph, interventions, counterfactuals Influence diagrams, credal networks, Markov random fields
Where the cost sits Conditional-independence tests, which grow with the conditioning set The junction tree. A large clique dominates the exact query

Neither search supplies a causal reading by itself.

bnlearn is the structure-learning catalogue behind labels such as MMPC and RSMAX. pyAgrum is the inference engine, and it also holds influence diagrams and credal nets. Do not quote a speed ratio between the packages. Tabu against constraint-based searches was Scutari’s comparison of algorithms, already on the search slide.

Quiz

❓ Fifteen questions on situations outside the two datasets, then the SAMPL draft.

Before the quiz ❓

Fifteen questions on new situations, not on the two datasets: four on the pitfalls, four on non-Gaussian responses, one on smoothing, two on the design, and four on the causal and Bayesian reading. Pick an option, then press x to check. Press q to reset that question.

Use the notation from the first hour: \(Y\) is the response, \(x\) is the covariate, \(\mu = \mathbb{E}(Y \mid x)\), and \(j\) is the unit that received the treatment.

About fifteen minutes, one minute a question. Ask the room before anyone checks. The check key is x. f still flips a flashcard, earlier in the deck. None of the fifteen needs CA-SYS or SPRUCE: the point is to transfer the rule to a study the room has not seen. If the clock is short, take questions 1, 5, 9, 10, and 13, one per block.

A ratio of 0.97 (0.95 to 0.99), with \(p < 0.05\)

  • A large effect, because the test rejects.
  • Detected, and small. Ask whether 3% matters.
  • Too uncertain to quote, because the interval is narrow.

The lab analysis failed for every soil core with pH below 4

pH is recorded for every core, including the cores with no result.

  • Missing completely at random: drop the cores.
  • Missing at random given pH. pH has to enter the model.
  • Missing not at random, so no model can use these rows.

Fertiliser dose split at its median into “low” and “high”

The dose was applied at eight levels, from 0 to 200 kg N per hectare.

  • Fine: two groups make the effect easier to explain.
  • Keep dose continuous, and allow a curve if the response bends.
  • Use three groups instead of two, to keep more information.

Significant in grasslands (\(p = 0.01\)), not in forests (\(p = 0.30\))

The same liming treatment was tested in both ecosystems.

  • The treatment works in grasslands only.
  • Estimate the difference of the two effects, with its interval.
  • Report both \(p\)-values side by side; the reader can compare.

Earthworms counted in quadrats of 0.25, 0.5, and 1 m²

You want the effect of tillage on earthworm density.

  • Fit a Poisson model to the raw counts, ignoring the area.
  • Poisson or negative binomial, with \(\log(\text{area})\) as an offset.
  • Divide each count by its area, then fit a Poisson to the densities.

Pearson \(\chi^2/\mathrm{df} = 10.6\) after a Poisson fit

The log-link rate ratio is the quantity you care about.

  • Take \(\log(Y+1)\) and fit a Gaussian linear model.
  • Keep the log link. Replace the Poisson variance.
  • Trust the Poisson interval: the mean model is right.

\(\exp(\hat\beta_1) = 4\) in a logit model of seedling survival

One-unit increase in centred soil moisture, other covariates held fixed.

  • The survival probability is multiplied by 4.
  • The odds of survival are multiplied by 4.
  • The log-odds increase by 4.

\(\exp(\text{mean of } \log Y)\) reported as the mean of \(Y\)

\(Y\) is soil organic carbon stock, positive and right-skewed.

  • Correct: exp undoes the log.
  • It estimates the median, below the mean. Correct for it, or fit a log-link GLM.
  • It overestimates the mean, because the log stretches small values.

A smooth of soil temperature reports \(\mathrm{edf} = 1.0\)

The basis had \(k = 10\) functions.

  • The smooth failed. Refit with a larger \(k\).
  • The penalty shrank the curve to a straight line. A linear term is enough.
  • Temperature has no effect.

Warming is set per open-top chamber

Four warmed chambers, four control chambers, and ten soil cores in each.

  • 80 cores: 40 replicates per arm.
  • Four replicates per arm. Cores are repeats inside \(j\).
  • Ten replicates, one for each core position.

Twenty plots run downhill along a moisture gradient

Four treatments, five plots each.

  • Assign the treatments in order down the slope.
  • Make five blocks along the slope, and randomise the four treatments inside each.
  • Randomise all twenty plots, and ignore the slope.

Hospital B is worse overall, and better inside each severity

A publishes 86% survival, B publishes 79%. Inside light cases, and again inside severe cases, B is higher.

  • Book A. The overall rate is the only estimand.
